EISIORIAM. Ting RKV. FaAtfCIS EL HAGEN, DIED NOVEILI3ER, 1881. A west and brilliant star tallen from it's sphere ; It shone with light from Heaven afar, And shed it's lustre here! Shone In the dusky night. On heart, and mini, and soul; Shone with a welcome guiding light. To lead on to the goal. The mystery of God, Taught by his subtle tongue, Cleared all but mercy from the road. And cheer'd the path with song! Rais'd in the darken'd path, A dime se: enely bright, And told of love that erst was wrath, ' With calm and pure delight. True messenger of Heaven, True lover of thy kind; To thee were talents richly given, The aroma of mini! Though great, with humble ni,en. Though good, with tearful eye; Through limy world, with vesture clean. Earth held him from the sky! Afar in stranger land, Away from luth and kin In lonely grave, on foreign strand, They kindly laid him in ! Ble-t shade,— when strangers bent Upon thy lonely bier, Thy requient the angels lent, And God, thy God. as near! Warrington
J. M.

_ One crack in the lantern may let in the wind to blow out the light; one leak unstopped will sink the ship and drown all on board; one unguarded point will cause rain of cha- racter. A Quaker's aivice to his son on his „wedding-day— " When thee want a-courtin', I told thee to keep thy eyes wide open I now thee is married, I tell thee to keep them half shut." A geutlena an who has occasion to walk with two ladies with one umbrella, should always go aiip the middle—that secures a drt coat to himself, and ía showing no, partiality to either of the ladies. • Richer!' Cobden, speaking once from the noble honour of his own upright soul, asked, thinking of a famous, success- ful, and unscrupulous statesman, "How will it be with him when all is retrospect ?" This is the great touchstone of life; bow it looks when regarded through all its long per- spective at a time when its chief actor has little Or no power to add to or improve the picture. A parson named Danger kept a public house on the Huntington road, near Cambridge. Oa being compelled to quit the house, which was not his own, he built an inn on the opposite side of the road, and caused to he painted on • the sign. "Danger from over the way." His successor in the old house retorted by inscribing over the door, " There Is no danger here now." A young lady was married in Louisville the other day, I and a newspaper account of the event was headed, "Mated in May." The New York Graphic suppoase that "Joined in June" and " Attiched in eiagrast': will be the fate of those who come later in the season. Likewise some will be "'Spliced in Seatemaer," "Orange-flowered in October," " Nuptial-toed in November," and "Doubled in December." On a saddlery-hardware shop in Baltimore is painted in large letters the follewing sign " Felioes, hubs, and spokes." A young woman Win the country, whose "in- tentions honors able--Iwhose parpoee marriage," walked hi, and mentioned t the gentlemanly clerk that he would.like to see sonic of the "fellows," and if any suited, would take a" huh." The gent!emanly clerk replied, that they were all be-" spoke" el:aside On one oceaeion, as Sterne entered a coffee-room at York, astrangsr, Airing him full in the face. insultingly said that he hatel a parson. Sterne instantly replied, "And so, sir, does my doe, for as I put on my gown and cassock be I ails a-barking." " Indee 1 ; and how long has he done so ?" aekd the stranger. "Ever since he was a puppy, sir," replied Sterne; "and you may depend upon it he will feel the same antipathy as long as be remains oae." It is said that one night, after a great battle, when his men were utterly exhausted, the great Napoleon was pacing about the camp and came upon a tired sentinel asleep. Then the Emperor took upon himself the obedience of the soldier, and paced his beat for him until he awoke, and then gave him back his musket. , That is Napoleon took the place of that Ben inel, doing his duty and suffering the pain of sleep- lessness in his stead, and so kept back from him the penalty for sleeping at his post. Nor A (Mincer, Sen.—Sitting beside the coachman on the box-seat I remarked, pointing to one of the leaders, "That near horse does not seem to draw much." "Not a hinch, sir," was the reply. "Why do you have him, then ?" I asks 1. "Because, you see, sir, this here's a four-horse coach, and he counts for one of 'ern." At last, after a young lady had sungs—and sung wet , too—it was noticed thatathe boy was silent and still. On neing asked why he did nct clap and call for an encore, he re:tliei, with a certain degree cf scorn, "Oh! she is my slat ir." Never tell people of several points at once—you will profit them nothing, but discourage them greatly. For in- stance, do not tell a man that he squints, has carroty hair, a Lightfal nose, distinguishing teeth, and is altogether a stutteringslool. Rather set his faults gradually before him, thus :—That though his eyes are crooked and his hair an nopleasing shade of red, he would not be 80 ill-looking if his nose were straight and his teeth less blackened by too much tasacco juice ; and that though he stammers pain- fully I speaking, that might be overlooked if he said any- thing worth listening to In this way he may hear what you h eve to say patiently and Witii advantage. The doctor's neckbands were too long for her ideas of ministerial ha- mill y, and, after a long harangue on the sin of pride' she intimated that she had brought a pair of scissors with her, and would be pleased if her dear pastor would permit her to cut them down to her notions of propriety. The doctot not only listened patiently, but handed over the offeading white bands to be operated upon. When she had cut them to her satisfactian and returned the bibs, it was the doctor's turn. "New," said he, "you must do me a good turn also." "Yes, that I will, doctor. What can it be f" "Well, you have something about you which is a deal too long, and •wia,eh causes me no end of trouble, and I should like to see it shorter." A story is current in Paris, illustrative of the readiness and tact of Alexander Dumas. Two playwrights, MM. Da Coney and Tb6au'on, had been requested to write a play called "Keen,' which they did, hat being unsatisfactory it was not accepted. The same preposition was made to Dames, who prcduced a piece that was successful, and is compensation the manager of the "Varieties" agreed that if toe first twenty-five performances gave to the treasury • 60,000 francs, Dames should be paid 1,000. "1 accepled Line proposition," said Dumas, "and at the twenty-fifth per- formance I entered his office, and asked. " Have you re- ceived 60,000 francs from the piece?' He answered, 'By Jove, you are an unlucky fellow, my dear author! I have just added the total receipts. We have 59,997 francs, Bowe lack three francs of the amount which would entitle you to , your compensation.' I said nothing. I quitted him, went ' to the ticket-office, and bought a parquet stall, which cost five francs. Then I returned to his office with my ticket in my hand, and said, 'You are an unlucky fellow, my dear manager; you have more than 60,000 francs in your treasury, for I have just purchased a five franc ticket.' He was a fellow of intelligence, so he opened his till and gave ins 1.000 francs." • PaOTECTIVE DEvICES IN THE FAUNA OE THE DESERT-- Animal life in the Sahara has various interesting features, among which the adaption of colour is specially notable. The general colour of the ground is, of course, that of sand, and the acanty, grey ish-leaved vegetation, away from oases, is hardly noticed, being covered with sand. Now, accord- ing to M. Vogt, one is struck, on coming from the coast, with the absence of all bright colours' red, green, and blue, in the animals ot the desert. With few exceptions, their hue approaches that of the ground. The adaptation is most remarkable in birds, reptiles, grasshoppers, rtc. Black and white exist in some animals—e.g., the male ostrich, which do not fear enemies; the female and young have some pro- tection in their dappled, brownish coat. There is a single —the coleoptera are nearly all black. exceptioa among insscts How ie this to be explained? M. Vogt says that these in- sects have a disagreeable smell, and that all of them, when in presence of clanger, feign death. In that contracted state they are exactly like the excrements of gazelles, goats, and sheep. "hie: With their odour, is thought to afford them surlicienfprotection. Again, a number of animals, chiefly fish, tut sigh crabe, larvae of insects, dic., are brought to the surf ice by the water of Artesian wells. M. Vogt looked in vain for any of the usual characters of subterranean crea- tures in these (blindnesit, Stc.), or, indeed, any difference from species in surface waters. This is explained by the fact that thee animals have only a temporary sojourn un- derground •' they pass down with the streams that partly disappear ter a time, in tunnels in the ground called bahts'' by the Arabs. My stock in trade will be ss. less in value than last year, but I am sure there is nothing about my farm that pays like the poultry.—Lake Diana. EFFECT OF FOOD AND AIR ON EGGS.—It does not re- quire much of any extra understanding on the part of any one to really see how the flesh of a fowl fed on wholesome food and water should be better to the taste than those fed at random and upon all manner of unwholesome food. This applies equally to the eggs also. Any one can test this if he so wishes quite easily by feeding on slop food, or food of an unclean kind, such as swill and decaying garbage. The flesh of such fowls will quickly taint and the eggs will taste unsavoury, at least to any one with an ordinary palate. Fresh air has much also to do with this matter. If any person of ordinary discernment would consider the actual condition of highly stalled animals of Christmas and other similar times of rejoicing, he would be quite easily satisfied that although to look at,the stall fed, animal, which always lacks pure ait, is the fattest, yet its flesh -does not agree with the stomach as does that of the healthy, ordinarily fed animal. Some say that the extra fat does this. I say not, for I have quite often kept account; and, though I do not touch a morsel of fat, I was troubled afterwards with a disordered stomach, which never happened when I partook heartily of fine beef, both fat and 'cwt.—Canada Farmer. AGRICULTURAL NOTES —A correspondent writes to a con- temporary :—"The mild dry weather of late has been favour- able for saving fodder and for field work. A few days ago I tea 4 through the best cropping district of West Lancashire, where the grain has all been cleared off the land and the potatoes all dug and removed, save in a few places where they are hogged' in the field. Turnips were fast being cleared away, and but a few fields of cabbages were visible. A good deal of stubble had been turne4 over by the plough, and on the harder wheat lands sowing is well advanced. Here and there a field has been 'breward'—that is, the blade has shot the clod. The land 'appears to be in capital con- dition for receiving the seed. The mossy ground which lie, between the 'sand ground' which belts the coast and the upper land is not in so advanced a condition as the higher land about Barscough and Ormskirk, which is probably owing to the rainy season some time ago. Where it is in very good heart and sheltered, grass land is uncommonly fresh and green for the season. Near the mouth of the Alt there is some grass which appears to he growing fast. Clover root generally appears to ho very thick, and affords a capital bite for the cattle, which in places are turned upon it. This will save fodder, which, judging from the hayricks, will be as scarce as was represented by the reports at the end of the slimmer. There is not so much haste to market hay this season as there was last, which is a hopeful sign that the farmrrs are not in the same urgent need of cash. The potato crop, from what I can gather, has not been found isd, heavy throughout as the haulm indicated, and the rot hii been very mischievous on some lands.- The report that a cargo of potatoes has been sent from this country to America wilt encourage the hope of better prices." EARTHWORMS.—The amount of earth brought up by worms from beneath the surf ace of the soil and aftetwards spread out more, or less completely by the rain gal wind ,may be judged by two methods—by the rate at which ob- jects left on the surface are buried, and more accurately by weighing the quantity. at. earth brought up in a given time As an example of the first method the following may be taken'—ln the spring of 3,835, a-. field, which had long existedans poor pasture and was so swampy that it fiembled slightly when stamped on, was thickly covered with red sand, so that the whole surface appeared at first bright red. Two and a half years afterwards holes were dug in the field, and the sand was found to form a layer at the depth of three.quartans of an inch from the surface. In 1842 fresh ' holes were dag, and then the red sand formed a distinct layer 2 inches beneath the surface, or 1 inch beneath the turf; so 'that, on an average, one-fifth of an inch of mould had been annually brought to the surface by the industry) of the earthworm. On a totally different soil, namely, on the chalk soils of Kent, Mr. Darwin found that the fine earth accumulated on the surface at about the same rate as in the case already given, that is, at an average rate of 02 to 0.22 of an inch per annum. But he observes that on the Kentish chalk, when a ploughed tield is first laid down in grass, the mould accumulates at a much slower rate. The ratef also, must become Very much slower after a bed of moill4 several inches thick has been formed; for the:worms then live chiefly near the surface, and burrow crown to a greater depth so as to bring up fresh earth from below only during winter when the weather is very cold, and during summer when it is very"dry. Among the instances illustra- tive of the weight of earth brought up by worms Mr. Dar- win gives the following t--In a field at the bottom of a valley in the chalk a square yard was measured at a spot, where large castings abounded. These castings, which re- tained perfectly their vermiform shape, were collected, and weighed, when partially dried, jib. inoz. This field hid been rolled with a heavy agricultural roller 52 days before, ' and this would certainly hive flattened every single casting on the land. The weather had been very dry for two or three weeks before the day of collection, so that not one casting appeared fresh or had been recently ejected. We may, therefore, assume that those which were weighed bad been ejected within, we will say, forty-five days from the time when the field was rolled. I had examined the same part of the field shortly before it was rolled, and it then abounded with fresh castings. Worms do not work in dry weather daring the summer, or in winter daring severe frosts. if we asaume that they work for only half the year —though this is too low an estimate—then the worms in thia field would eject during the year 83 37 pounds per I square yard; or 18.12 tons per acre, assuming the whole I surface to be equally productive in castings. As this enor- mous weight of earth would pass through the intestines a the warms, its fertility would necessarily be greatly In- creased. In three other cases the observed or calculated weights of the ejects per acre per annum were found to bel 14.58, 756, and 161 tons respectively. Supposing the an- nual castings to be strewn over the ground in a layer of uniform thickness, the accumulation of mould in a period of ten yeas was calculated in five examples of different kinds of soil to attain respective depths of 2.2, 1.9, 2.1, 2.2, and 0 83 inches.

Drainage, clean cal- foreign corn." That would certainly be the best plan of tivation, manures of the more lasting kinds, and the costly keeping up the rich man's rents, but it would be at the in- and skilful formation of a suitable live stock, each demand creased cost of the Poor males loaf. Sir Stafford Northoote refers to Fair Trade or Protection veils in" Scotland, and is already found on well managed simply as "pious opinions ;" and, further stillo the high properties in England, tike Lord Leicester's and the Crown priest of Toryism—the Marquis of SalishurY—told his estates." " The belt land system for us is the one which audience at Newcastle that "the food of the people must be giVes most inducement to spend roomy wisely on the land, held sacred." and, before he does that, the English farmer is justly en- What, then, can be done for the British farmer? We titled to some reasonable assurance that he cannot be turned have recently seen an Act passed for the benefit of the Irish off his farm at short notice, and his invested capital "con- farmer, giving him, in effect, what are known as the fiscated " by the landlord. , "Three F's"—Fixity of Tenure, Fair Rents, and Free Sale Legislation must provide for some degree of "Fixity of of Tenant Right. Now, the writer has within the last 15 Tenure," taking full care that while good tenants are pro- years spent a deal of time in different parts of Ireland, and tected against bad landlords, good ',landlords are protected has had special opportunities of studying the Land Clues- against bad tenants. tion there; but, while quite admitting that the Land Ques- tion in Ireland is dissimilar in many respects to the Land Question on this side of the water, cannot a modified form of the "Three F's," sueh as our circumstances require, be introduced into this country? It is not, surely, contended that our law-abiding farmers are not entitled to equal legal protection as their more, excitable Irish brethren. Let us review the present position of the English Farmer, and the necessity for reform with regard to the first F. One of the first thiags which arrests the attention of any- one studying our present system is that Insecurity of Ten ire is the rule and not the exception—i.e., a large pro- portion of farmers are yearly tenants only, liable to be turned out at six months' notice. How has this origi- nated? Mr. Broderick, in his recent work, " English Land and English Landlords," assumes that tenancy at will existed in every stage of our agricultural history, but goes on to show that a new and powerful motive for re fusing leases was created by the Reform Act of 1832. Under the so called " Chandos Clause" or eection 20 of that Act every tenant of a farm paying a rent of £5O or upwards for the first time acquired the county franchise. Thenceforward the political influence of landlords was multiplied by the votes of their farm tenants, and, in order to maintain that influence, it was thought necessary to keep farm tenants in a state of dependence by letting farms only from year to year. Doebtless the confidence inspired by the liberal management of many great hereditary properties, as well as a wholesome dread of periodical valuations incident to a system of leases, have done mach to make English farmers content with a tenure under which the great Adam Smith declared that it is against all reason and probability to ex- pect an occupier to improve the soil, and which Scotch far- mers have long since declined. The importance attached to rights of sporting in England often induces landlords to ac- cept low rents from non-improving tenants, who can be turned out at short notice if they meddle with the game; and the power of distress enables them to dispense with too strict inquiries into a. tenant's skill and capital. By the operation of these and other causes it is tolerably certain that yearly tenancy has become the role and leasehold tenure the exception in most English counties. We have many good, landlords in England, or this would not have been tolerated so long; but, speaking of yearly tenancies in Ireland, Lord Dufferin, himself an Irish land- lord, said in the House of Lords, "What is the spectacle presented to us by Ireland? It is that of millions of per- sons, whose only dependence and whose chief occupation is agriculture, for the most part cultivating their lands—i.e., sinking their past, their present, and their future upon yearly tenancies. But what is a yearly tenancy? 'Why, it is an impossible tenure—a tenure which, if its terms were to be literally interpreted, no Christian man would offer and none but a madman would accept." We look forward to the time when there will not be a yearly tenancy of farm land in the United Kingdom, *hen no farmer shall be "under the thumb" or subject to the Whim or caprice of either the landlord or his agent, so long as the farmer does what is right, i.e., pays his rent regu- larly and keeps hi' farm in good condition. Now that farmers have the protection' of the 'Ballot Act, landlords cannot make.sure of their tenants' votes, even though they are liable to six months' notlee to quit, for the day has gone past when farmers can be driven, to the polling booth like sheep. No, we hold with Lord Derby, who once said at South- port "I think every good ten Ant who is expected to stay permanently on the farm he holds is entitled to ask for a lease from the proprietor. It is a very simple alternative if a man is not fit to settle on an estate with a lease, he is not fit to settle without one; if he cannot be trusted with a lease, he cannot be trusted with the land, I say this—and in what I am saving I am rather in my own mind address- ing landlords than tenants,—l say if a tenant is to be ex- pected to lay out capital on his farm, it implies no distrust of the landlord—it is simply an ordinary and proper busi- ness precaution—that he should insist on having some leaae. I believe that these two things—one the making the giving of a lease a general rule, and the other having leases drawn more simply than as a rule they are at present— would go very far to settle that question of land ownership 'of which we have heard something of late." But what has been the case? In past years, when agricultural matters were prosperous, there was a keen competition for farms, and when one fell vacant there were twenty applicants, and the landlords were able to dictate their own terms, however One-sided they might be, and there was sure to be some one foolish enough, or so situated, as to be obliged to accept them, trusting to good seasons and luck to weather along, notwithstanding the stringent terms of his lease, if one was granted him. There are leases and leases. Some of them are a curse to the farmer, tie him down hand and foot,and regulate his cultivation of the farm by ideas which were in vogue a generation or two ago. They are often prepared by lawyers, who know no more about scientific farming than our I own desks, but sirftply follow the precedents in what are called "Books of Style," which may have been in their 1 offices for many a long year. They dictate to a nicety the irotation of crops, irrespective of the difference of climate, rainfall, soils, situation, drc., the principle being to take care the tenant can get no advantage. The duties of many land' agents or stewards are to collect the rents•at fixed times, see that the land is not what is called " miscropped," and that no hay, straw, or other produce is sold off, or otherwise that manure is bought in return. Many good agents who know what humbug all this is, cannot break down the rules of the estate. When ttese old-fashioned regulations were first drawn up, artificial manures, oil cake, and feeding stuffs were unknown, and it is ridiculous keeping up antiquated restrictions hindering a tenant from doing the best for him- self and his farm, under such altered circumstances. Tenants have to grow corn when they know they ought to grow grass, and turnips when they ought to have corn, and the only reason given is, "I am bound to a rotation." No `matter how much a farm might be benefited by a ahange of cropping, in few cases are farmers allowed to think for themselves—they must keep on in the track chalked out. It Is laid down not only what they may grow, but what they may sell. Straw a few years ago was worth several pounds a ton in some districts. No matter—in many cases it must be used on the premises at a dead loss. The same as to tur- nips, and sometimes tenants are only allowed to grow euffi- cient patatoes for their own use. How different, however, are the leases on the Norfolk farms of the Earl of Leicester. The tenancy is for 20 years, from the 11th day of October. It is to be terminable at the end of 16 years at the request of the tenant, and with the consent of the landlord, the intention being that if both Parties desire it, a new lease may be granted from the end of the 16th year for another term of 20 years, at the old rent for the four remaining years of the original term, and thence- forth at a rent to be fixed by agreement. During the first 16 years the tenant may cultivate according to his own judgment; during the last four, if he should fail to renew, he must cultivate on the four-course system. Lord Tolle- mache, on his Helmingham estates, gives what is called a " Lease Note," binding the landlord to allow the tenant un- disturbed possession of his farm, without any increase of rent for 21 years, upon condition of his keeping the land in a good state of cultivation, and draining or boning a certain number of acres. Under such a Lease Note, while the tenant remains free to throw up his farm, the landlord resigns the power of giving him notice to quit, unless upon a breach of the conditions. Again, in Scotlandathe Earl of Fife allows his tenants, who all hold leases, to pursue the course of tillage that is likely to pay best, the only exceptions being that it is prohibited to reap two white crops in succession, while it is enacted that upon the expiry of a lease, the land must be left under some regular rotation of cropping, so that a new tenant shall not be subjected to a disadvantage. Any one will see at a glance what advantages the tenants have on the above estates, which cannot but redound to the benefit of the landlord, for what can be better for him than prosperous contented tenants, and it is no wonder that the first Earl of Leicester, in responding to a toast at his own table, said: "Gentlemen, some of us landowners are proud of our stock, some of our dogs, some of our ancestry, but for myself, I am proud of my tenants." Free cultivation is not a new idea. One hundred years ago Archdeacon Paley argued that to admit of good farm- ing, the occupier ought to have all the power over the soil that is necessary for its perfect cultivation ; or, as a recent writer has said, Landowners must move with the times, and throw the restrictions which are in force on their pro- perty to the winds. They must allow their tenants to farm their lands as the more advanced schools of agriculture suggest; they must allow farmers to sell what they grow, and make the most of everything they can produce. Ido not mean that farmers may Fell off all that grows on the land, and buy nothing back; this would mean ruin to land and landowners very soon; but what I would insist on Is that so long as a farmer manages his land well, keeps it clean, and altogether farms compatibly with good hus- bandry, he ought to be allowed to do as he chooses." Why cannot something like what the above noblemen have done voluntarily on their own estates, in the way of granting good leases, amounting to a sort of fixity of tenure, be made the law of the land ? It is a well-known fact that the best agriculture is found on farms whose tenants are protected by good leases; the next best, on farms whose

M I SCELLAN EOUS, The election at Stafford, on Saturday, resulted in the return of Mr. Salt, the Conservative candidate, who formerly represented the borough, by a majority of 297 over his oppo- nent, Mr. George Howell. A Miss Gafford, who held two farms near Killinck, county Wexford, was found dead in bed on Sunday morning. She is supposed to have been strangled, and it is said that a box in her room had been broken open. Mr. Bright, acknowledging congratulations from Warwick on his birthday, says it required five years' teaching and agitation to induce the country to demand free trade in bread, and it would take many mere to induce it to reverse that policy. A fire occurred on Monday at Messrs. Jeffrey's paper staining works, Essex Road Islington, London. The works were destroyed, and two shops and four houses adjoining were also much damaged by fire and water. The damage is estimated at between £39,000 and £40,000. Mrs. Besant was the Gnly student who this year obtained a first-class certificate in the examinations at South Ken- sington in the advanced stage of general biology. Twelve students VI ent up for examination, Mrs. Besant passing first- class, six students passing second-class, and five failing. The examiners were Professors Huxley and Foster. Mr. W. Summers, M.P., addressing his constituents at Dukinfield, on Monday evening, dealt chiefly with the Irish land question and the Free Trade policy of this country. He said that the Irish Land Act was a measure which would make the present Administration memorable in history. The retaliation proposals of the Fair Traders he regarded as impossible. At Birmingham, on Monday, a bailiff named Charles Blikemoor, was committed for trial forattempting to murder his wife. The prisoner went home so drunk on Saturday that he fell to the floor, exclaiming, "Like a soldier I fall."

BIRTH AND DEATH RATE IN THE UNITED KINGDOM. In the United Kingdma the births of 278,170 children, and the deaths of 143,518 persons, were registered in the three months ending 30th September, 1881. The recorded natural increase of population was thus 134,652. The re. gistered number of persons married in the quarter ending 30th June, 1881, was 122,052. The birth-rate in the United Kingdom in the third quarter of 1881 was 316 per 1,000, and the death-rate 163. The marriage-rate in the second quarter of 1881 was 140 per 1,000. MARRIAGES.—Daring the three months ending June last the marriages of 100,400 persons were registered in England and Wales; these were equal to an annual rate of 15.5 per 1,000. This was 10 below the average rate in the corre- sponding period of the ten years 1871-80; it considerably exceeded, however, the rates that prevailed in the second quarters of 1879 and 1880, which were so low as 14 7 and 14,3. The marriage-rate, which has declined from 18.3 in the second quarter of 1873 to 14-3 in the corresponding period of 1880, showed a decided recovery in the three months ending June last. The annual marriage-rate during the last-mentioned quarter ranged in the several English counties from 97 and 101 in Huntingdonshire and Hertford- shire to 17 3 in Lancashire, 17.5 in Lincolnshire, 17.9 in Northumberland, and 185 in Nottinghamshire. . . .

BIRTII9.—The births registered during the three months , ending September last were 215,586, and 3,437 fewer than in the corresponding quarter of last year. The annual birth- rate did not exceed 32.8 per 1,000 of the estimated popula- tion, which was 1.8 below the average rate in the correspond- ing periods of the 10 years 1871-80, acd was lower than in the third quarter of any year since 1860. The birth-rate last quarter did not exceed 27.8 in Huntingdonshire; it ranged upwards to 356 in Lancashire, 36 0 in Nottingham- shire, and 38.4 in Durham. In twenty of the largest Eng- lish towns the birth-rate ranged from 295 and 31-0 in Brighton and Norwich to 37 0' in Liverpool and Sheffield 37-7 in Salford. In fifty other large town districts the rate averaged 34-3-; the lowest rate in this district was 26-0 in Cheltenham, and the highest were 411 in Dudley and Bar- row-in-Furness and 41-5 in Bolton.

DEATITS.—During last quarter 109,956 deaths were re- gistered in England and Wales, showing a decline of 21,285 from the number in the corresponding period of 1880. The annual death-rate during the three months ending Septem. ber last did not exceed 16.7 per 1,000 of the population, and was no less than 2 9 below the average rate in the ten preceding corresponding quarters. In the third or summer quarter of 1879 the English death-rate was so low as 16 3 ; with this single exception the rate last quarter was lower than in any summer quarter since civil registration com- menced in 1837. The average death-rate in the third or summer quarters of the 43 years 1838-80, was equal to 204 per 1,000; the recorded rate last quarter was 31 below this rate, implying that more than 24,000 persons survived the three-months who would have died, had the death-rate cor- responded with the average rate in the 43 preceding cor- responding quarters. The 109,956 deaths included 57,099 of males and 52,857 of females; the annual death-rate among males was equal to 17-9, and among females to 151 per 1,000 estimated to be living of each sex. In equal numbers living the deaths were as 114 of males to 100 of females: in the third quarter of 1880 this proportion WU 115 to 100. The annual death-rate among persons of both sexes in the several English counties ranged from 12.5 both in Herefordshire and Dorsetshire, to 194 in Nottingham- shire and 201 in Leicester.hire. _ .

In the districts comprising the chief towns, and contain- ing an estimated population of fifteen and a half millions of persons, the death-rate was equal to 18 5 per 1,000; in the remaining and chiefly rural population of about ten and a half millions, the rate did not exceed 142 per 1,000. These urban and rural rates were respectively 3.2 and 24 below the average rates in the ten preceding corresponding quarters. In equal numbers living, the deaths in the urban were as 130 to 100 in the rural population. In twenty of the largest English towns, including London, the death-rate averaged 20.5 per 1,000, and was 27 below the rate that prevailed in the third quarter of last year. In fifty other English and Welsh town districts, the death-rate averaged only 169, and was 3•6 below the mean rate in the twenty larger towns. The 109,956 deaths last quarter included 29,765 of infants under one year of age, 54,516 of children and adults aged between one and 60 years, and 25,675 of persons aged up- wards of 60 years. The rate of infant mortality, measured by the proportion of deaths under one year to births re- gistered, was equal to 138 per 1,000; in the ten preceding corresponding quarters the proportion of infant mortality averaged 170 per 1,000, and ranged from 115 in 1879 to 195 in 1880. Excepting the summer of 1877, infant mortality was lower in the three months ending September last than in the third quarter of any recent year. In the twenty large towns the proportion of infant mortality averaged 187 per 1,000, it ranging from 125 in Bristol to 325 in Leicester. In the fifty other town districts , infant mortality averaged only 143 per 1,000, and was 144 below the rate in the twenty large towns. The annual rate of mortality among persons aged between one and sixty years was equal to 9.3 per 1,000 persons esti- mated to be living at these ages, against an average of 107 in the ten preceding corresponding quarters. Among per- sons aged upwards of sixty years the annual death-rate averaged only 523 per 1,000, and was 31 below the average rate in the ten preceding summer quarters; this rate was lower than that prevailing in any of these ten correspond- ing quarters, the nearest approach to it being 53.2 in 1879. The rate of mortality at all ages last quarter was 15 per cent, below the average rate in the ten preceding corres- pending quarters; the decline was equal to 18 per cent. among infants under one year of age, 13 per cent, among children and adults aged between one and sixty, and 5 per cent, among persons aged upwards of sixty years. The 109,956 deaths from all causes included-8,307 diar- rhoea, 3,535 scarlet fever' 2,031 whooping-cough, 1,705 fever, 1,341 measles, 674 smallpox, 629 diphtheria, total 18,222, a death-rate from them of 2.77, against an average rate of 4-21 for the ten preceding corresponding quarters. Only in one of these ten summer quarters was the death- rate from these diseases lower than in the quarter just past, namely, in 1879, when the cold season and consequent ab- sence of summer diarrhcea reduced the rate to 2.25. The rate was 415 in the twenty great towns and 2-55 in the fifty other considerable towns. The most prevalent of the zy- motic diseases, as is the rule in the summer quarter, was diarrheas. This caused 8,307 deaths, an annual rate of 1.26 per 1,000, against an average for the ten preceding summer quarters of 2.27. Once only in these ten years was the summer diarrhoea rate lower than this, namely, 1879, when it was only 0.73. The low rate in the past quarter was doubtless attributable to the cold weather that prevailed through August and September, and which more than coun- terbalanced, so far as the production of diarrhoea was con- cerned, the burst of excessive heat and high diarrhoea morr talky of July. The deaths from scarlet fever were 3,535, and the death-rate was 0 54, the average rate for the ten preceding summer quarters having been 0.62. The mor- tality from whooping-cough is almost invariably at its minimum in the summer quarter, and the past was no ex- ception to the rule. The deaths due to it were 2,031, which correspond to an annual rate of 0.31, the average rate for the ten preceding summer quarters having been 0.36. The deaths ascribed to fever, including typhus, enteric, simple, and ill-defined forms of fever were 1,705, corresponding to an annual rate of 0 26, against an average of 0.44 for the ten preceding corresponding quarters. Once only in those ten summers was the rate so low as in the past quarter, namely, in 1879, when it was also 0.26. The lowest county rate was 05 in Herefordshire, whilst the highest was 0.49 in East Riding; in Wigan it was 0.82, and in St. Helens 118. The deaths from measles were 1,341, corresponding to an annual rate of 020, against an average rate of 0'26 for the ten preceding summer quarters. In counties the rate varied from 000 in Herefordshire, Westmorland, and Huntingdonshire, to 033 in Oxfordshire, and 0-36 in Lan- cashire. In the twenty great towns the rate was 0 51, and 007 in the fifty other considerable towns. In Liverpool it was as high as 1•70. Among sub-districts with an excessive mortality from this disease were Portland, Harwood, Barns- ley. The deaths from diphtheria were 629, corresponding to an annual rate of 010, against an average rate of 0.09 for the ten preceding summers. The deaths from smallpox, which bad been 730 and 1,213 in the two immediately preceding quarters, fell, as is the rule in the summer quarter, and were only 674. This, how- ever, is a higher number than in any summer quarter since the great outbreak in 1871 and 1872. Of the 674 deaths no less than 461 occurred in London and, 61 more in the Outer Ring, while of the remainder a considerable propor- tion occurred in the immediately adjoining counties. There were, however, 34 deaths in Lancashire and 15 in Yorkshire, and a localised outbreak causing nine deaths occurred in the sub-district of Wokinglaim. In 174 of the 461 deaths that occurred in London no reliable information was obtainable as to previous vaccination; of the remaining 287, as to which the necessary information was forthcoming, 108, or 37.6 per cent., were certified to have been vaccinated, while no less than 170, or 62.4 per cent., were certified to have been unvaccinated.

MONDAY.—Before the. Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and " Ex-Ma; lr (Councillor Fairclough.) RUNNING I) '2.oNs."-Michael Rabbitt, a young man, was charged with Oeing drunk and disorderly on the previous : 019 Antler, who proved the case, said the prisone Vas "running drunk."—Mr. White (magistrates' &lett) ; What do you mean by "running drunk ?"—Witness: Re could ran better than he could walk. (Laughter.)—Mr. Wbite: He was obliged to keep running, afraid that if he stood still he might fall down, I suppose. (Laughter.)— Prisoner was fined ss. and costs. STTOCKING illtarriarrr.—A rough looking young fellow named John Hennessy, was charged with being drunk anci disorderly in Horsernarket-street, with assaulting P.C.'s Hell ingworth, and Hennessy, and Thomas and W. Richard- son.—Themas Hogan was charged with attempting to re- scue the prisoner, and assaulting P.C. Hollingworth.—The Chief Constable said that about seven o'clock on Saturday night, prisoner Hennessy was illtreating another man, who was very drunk and weak, in Horse- marker-street, where a large crowd had collected. Thomas Richardson, who was near asked Hen- nessy "Are you going to kill the man," and pullid him off, when Hennessy savagely kicked him. Coming to his brother's aid, William was also assaulted, and with difficulty got away. Then, "as was too often the case," a policeman , came when the row was over, and took the prisoner whom he knew away. Again at nine o'c.ock Hennessy was creat- , inga disturbance in Horsemarket-street, and P.C. Holling- worth took him into custody. Prisoner struck him with his fists, and a number of people in the large crowd which surrounded them, seized the officer by the legs and pulled him to the ground, whilst in that position prisoner kicked him savagely about the legs and body. Hogan attempted to rescue the prisoner and assaulted P.C. Hennessy who had gone to the assistance of P.C. Hollingworth. Four officers were required to take prisoner to the police office, and over half a dozen to keep off the crowd.—Corroborative evi- dence was given, and Hennessy said he knew nothing of , the assault. Hogan denied the attempt at rescue.—llen- nes*, was committed to gaol for tkree months with hard labour for the assault on the officers, and for two months f,or the assault on Messrs. Richardson.—Hogan was committed for two months. _ .

Fnermuraorr ENLISTMENT.—John Taylor, alias Charles Barrett, a soldier, was charged with making a false state- ment On being attested. He had sworn before the magis- trates on the 20th October, that he had not previously served i the army, when he had been discharged with ignominy from the 20th Regiment of foot in May, 1878.—He was sentenced to three months' hard labour. SHAMEFUL CONDTTT TO A WOMAN—Thomas Griffin, a young man, was charged with an aggravated avault upon Amelia O'Brien, a woman who appeared to have been badly abused.—When enquiring from a woman in Orford-lava, on Sunday, as to where she could obtain good lodgings, complainant was assaulted by the prisoner and two other young men, who had not been apprehended, and said " We will find you a place." They took her to a house in Silver-square, where they attempted to take liberties with her, and the prisoner struck her on the face with his fist. lie then seized the poker, but it was taken from him. Complainant screamed loudly, and P.C. Shaw was fetched by the prisoner's grand- mother. The officer attempted to enter the house, but the door was locked, the key being held from a bedroom window in a tantalising manner. When be was about to break open the door, they opened it and he released the woman. She had been badly used and her mouth was full of blood.—The Mayor said it was a most outrageous assault, and committed prisoner to gaol for six months with hard labour, and ordered him to find two sureties to keep the peace for six menths longer, or in default an additional six months' imprisonment. —Before the rising of the court, the other two young men were apprehended and charged with the assault. They were named Martin Griffin, and Patrick McDonald.—Complainant said the prisoners acted in an improper manner, burdid not strike her.—Prisoners were committed to gaol for two months with hard labour. _ _ .

UNREGISTERED LODGING HousEs.—Martin Dolan, was fined 55. for keeping an unregistered lodging-house, and a Penalty of 108. each was imposed upon Robert Groves and Martin Peacock for a similar offence. NEGLECTED EDIXITION.—A fine of ss. was inflicted upon each of the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—Amos Bramall, cutter, Dial-court; John Painter, tanner, Morris's-court ; John Broderick, tanner, 27, Dolmans-lane. Thomas Ellison, • iron- worker, Powys-street. John Reedy, labourer, 5, Carlisle- street ; John Bowden forgeman, John-street; John Corfield ; forgeman, 153, Dailam-lane ; William Blanchard, Bank- quay ; Pat Dolly, joiner, Blackhurst-street ; Lawrence Lan,forgeman, Portland-street; John Maloney, brewer, Cock hedge; Thomas Garritty, labourer, Jolley'.B-yard. WEDNESDAT.—Before Alderman Davies and Councillor

Fairclaugh. THE Box Into WANTED TO EMIGRATE.—John Henry Kearney (15) was charged with stealing from the dwelling- house of his parents, 3, Fennell-street, on Monday, £6 in gold, and 31. 6i in silver, their property.—lt appeared that the prisoner until recently worked at the Whitecross Wire Works, but he got the "sack," and as he had not sufficient money to take borne he went to lodge on Friars' Green. The parents got to hear of his whereabouts, and induced him to return home. He came in regularly for his meals but did not work. The father, a joiner, had been out of work for 12 months, and the mother succeeded in main- taining a family of 9 persons by selling old clothes in the il-clea'onrrk r one side f i bat transactions,wasfoundthe "mto on day aeye week's prisoner L G she _ had decamped, and that me Pau go.— log that the lad had awdesire to go to America the lii Ii communicated with Mr. Hunt, the chief constable, who gave her a letter to the Liverpool police authorities. Mrs. Kearney proceeded to Liverpool on Tuesday, and had just left a detective when she saw her boy gazing at a placard. She drew the detective's attention and the lad was appre- hended. A telegram was despatched to Warrington, and P.S. James went over to Liverpool and received the prisoner into custody. The sergeant learned that the lad had taken 1 a passage to America by the National Line, for which he had paid half fare, representing himself as 11 years of age. He succeeded in getting the money returned less the com- mission, and also the cost of an outfit the prisoner had pur- chased in Water-street. The money he received, together with some the prisoner had in his possessien, amounted to more than the sum reported stolen; and on being asked to account for this the lad said be had saved 183. of it.—The mother, in reply to the Bench, said she had never known the prisoner to do anything wrong before; and the prisoner said he had starved himself to save his money. It was his in- tion to make for Pittsburg.—The case was adjourned for 14 days. THIIRSDAY.—Before Alderman Webster, and Councillor _ Milner.

FRXDAY.—Before Messrs. H. S. Hall and 'l'. rilkinglOn. IMPUDENT FRAUD ON THE RAILWAY COMPANY. Wm. Jones, beerhouse keeper, of Thatto Heath, was charged with riding on the London and North-Western Railway with intent to avoid payment of fare, on the 31st Qctober and the sth November.—Mr. Ferrand prosecuted, and said de- fendant had carried on a systematic and impudent course of fraud on the railway company, and if their worships were satisfied on hearing the evidence, that the defendant had committed the frauds, he should ask that the full penalty in both cases be inflicted—Defendant pleaded " partially " guilty to the first charge, and guilty to the latter, but after- wards admitted that he had done wrong, and he was "sorry for it."—James Wilkinson, a detective in the service of the company, said that he was specially set to watch the defendant. On the 31st October, he watched defendant leave his house at Thatto Heath and go to the station. De- fendant entered a carriage without having paid for, and received a ticket, and witness got into a carriage with him, mid rode with him to Wigan where the defendant left the carriage. Witness also got out and watched the defen- dant's movements on the platform. After walking about the platform for fifteen minutes' defendant went behind some cagines and got into the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway siding. Witness followed and apprehended him in the presence of a ticket collector at Wigan whom he had apprised of his (witness's) scheme as soon as he had got out of the carriage. Defendant gave a wrong address, saying that he lived At Manchester. It was true that he formerly carried on the business of a hatter at Manchester. On the sth November witness was on the St. Helens platform when defendant got out of the train. On being asked for his ticket by Lennon, the ticket collector, he replied that he had not come by train. He was allowed to go off the platform, and immediately afterwards Was arrested by witness. He then admitted that he had come by train.—Defendant said that many times there was no one at the gateway to collect tickets.—The Bench asked if the company only wished a conviction on one case.—Mr. Ferrand said he must press for the heaviest penalty in both cases, and also asked that something be allowed for the four witnesses, because he could tell their worships a great deal about the defendant's movements if he liked.—The Bench fined the defendant £2 13s. 6d. (including costs) in each case,—altogether £5 75., or two months' imprisonment. The money was at once paid. BIGAMY BY A ST. HELENS MAY. Joseph Newton, formerly manager of the St. Helens Liberal Club, was charged with marrying Esther Westhead on the 26th Octo- ber, his former wife, Mary Newton, being then alive.—Ann Whittle, an elderly single woman, said she knew the priso- ner. She was present at his marriage with Mary Newton about twenty years ago, in the Lowe House Church. Mary Newton was now alive.—Elizabeth Steele, wife of the clerk

of St. James's Church, Liverpool, said she was present when the wedding ceremony was being performed. Prisoner gave his address as " Upper Parliament-street ;" and a man named Norman acted as best man and a woman named Murphy as bridesmaid.—P.C. Cottam said he apprehended prisoner on the previous night in Lyon-street, and informed him that he had better go with him to the police office, as he had a charge of bigamy to prefer against him. Prisoner replied, "All right ; I was expecting it." At the p dice station he charged prisoner with marrying Esther Westhead. Ile replied, "Yes."-.-Prisoner pleaded guilty, and said he expected Mr. Massey appearing for him, but as that gentle- man had not turned up he would reserve his defence. He asked for bail, and the Bench said they would allow him out on substantial bail, notice of which was to be given within 24 hours.—Prisoner failed to obtain sureties, and was sent to gaol where lie will wait until the next assize court at Liverpool.

MONDAY.—Before Captain Willis and Mr. W. L. Evans. AN OLD OFEENDER.—Elizabeth Lawrenson made her thirty-fifth appearance at this court, and her twelfth this year, and was charged with being drunk in Liverpool-road. —Fined 10s. and costs., or 14 days imprisonment. SLEEPING OCT.—Three boys named Thomas Jeffrey, Frank Grime, and Alfred Campbell were charged with sleeping out, having no visible means of subsistence, at a quarter past two that morning. P.C. Hamilton found pri- soner's asleep in Mr. Mooney's glass works.—Jeffrey and Grime were sent to prison for seven days ; anl Campbell, who had run away from the workhouse where he had been sent for four years for sleeping out, was sent to prison for 14 days. RESISTING THE POLICE. Michael McDermot was charged with being drunk and disorderly, also with assault- ing P.C. Mitchell, and further with resisting P.C. Cottam whilst in the execution of his duty.—P.C. Cottam said that at twenty minutes to nine on Saturday night, the 12th inst., defendant was drunk and disorderly iu Liverpool-street, Eccleston. There was also a man named Michael Delaney drunk at the same time and place. Delaney was so dis- orderly that he was obliged to take him into custody. McDermot then got hold of Delaney by the arm and said, "What are you going to do with him." Witness told him, and McDermot demanded that Delaney be let go, and he would take him home. Witness said that he could not do so, and at the same time McDermot tried to pull Delaney away. McDermot tried io knock Mitchell down, and attempted to prevent witass from putting the snaps on Delaney. Witness asked the crowd to take McDermot away and they did so, by force.—P.G. Mitchell gave similar evidence.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, who appeared on behalf of 'the defendant, said that he would bring witnesses to prove that defendant was not drunk, and that he was taking Delaney, who was tlle wjing for drink, home. They both lived at the Vditalt&tille most trivial assault-I'hr the police this was —James Cunningham, Patrick Fagan, Patrick Quiritad, Margaret McDermot (wife of defendant), and Martin Quinn gave evidence to the effect that defendant was not drunk.— The Bench did not think the case of drunkenness was proved, but they considered that resisting the police was a serious thing, and they would inflict a penalty of 20s. and costs. The case of assault would be dismissed. SELLING ADULTERATED MrsTemo.—Michael McGee, pro- vision dealer, Liverpool-street, was charged with selling two ounces of mustard which was not of the substance and nature of the quality demanded.—lnspector Johnston said that on the 25th October he went to defendant's shop. Defendant was a provision dealer on a very large scale. He asked defendant for two ounces of mustard, for which he paid lid. Having received it, he said he was about to send it to the public analyst to be analysed, and that if defen- dant chose witness would divide it into three parts—one to be sent to the analyst, another defendant could keep, and the third witness would keep ;otherwise he would send it to the analyst as it was. Defendant chose the latter process, and witness at once sealed it up in defendant's presence, and sent it with Sherratt, his assistant, to the county analyst (Dr. Campbell Brown), who sent him a certificate stating that a quarter of the mustard sent was not mustard.—De- fendant said he bought the mustard at Mr. Ellison's sale in Church-street. No shopkeeper was supposed to be able to test mustard.-1 penalty of 40s. and costs was inflicted. FAWNING ANOTHER'S PROPERTY.—Maria Preston, who did not appear, was summoned for illegally pawning a black silk dress, the property of Mrs. James, wife of the landlord of the Star Inn, Mertonbank-lane.—Mr. Riley appeared on behalf of the prosecutrix, who, he said, out of compassion had at various times entrusted articles to the defendant to repair. In July last prosecutrix handed a black silk dress to her to be altered in shape, and on the 6th September she. heard that defendant had pawned it at Mr. Royle's shop.— Fined £2 3s. 61. (including cost of dress), or one Month's

- A MISCELLANEOUS COLLECTION.—A widow named Mary Ann Rete, residing at 26, Dallam-lane, was charged with stealing from the stall of Margaret Boot, in the market, a child's pinafore, value 3d. ; from William Friar, two tele- phones and a pair of earrings worth Is. ad.; from John Leach, three purses, value 7d. ; and a small loeking-glass, value id, from John Blackbean.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was seen to go to the several stalls, and steal the articles in a "most barefaced" manner. Information was given to B.C. Chantler' who apprehended her.—Prisoner was com- mitted to gaol for two months. NEGLECT OF FAMILY.—Peter Swift, a mechanic, was charged with neglecting to maintain his family. Mr. liar- bourne said the prisoner's child had been in the workhouse twelve months, and the prisoner had paid nothing towards his maintenance, although he had been in regular work for 13 weeks. The amount owing was £l3. Prisoner had pre- viously been convicted of a similar offence. Prisoner said ' he would pay the money if allowed time, but Mr. Ilarbourne said he was sure he would not. The Bench committed him to gaol for two months with hard labour.--William Dut- ton, an ironworker, was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and family. On the previous (lay, prisoner's wife applied to the Guardians for relief and they granted her 10s., at the same time giving Mr. Harbourne instructions to pro- secute the prisoner. No notice had been given to the prisoner, who was living apart from his wife with two chil- dren. Mr. Moore, who defended, characterised it as a hard case to deal with a man in so summary- a manner, and promised to pay the money, and make an allowance to the wife. On this understanding the Bench adj iurned the case for a fortnight. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. John White (chairman) and Captain Litton. There was no business of public interest.

imprisonment. THE SACREDNESS or PROEERTy.—James Hunt, John Swift, John Wilcock, and Richard Tunstall, lads, were charged with damaging a wall at Blackbrook, the property of David Bromilow & Co.—From the evidence of a witness named Taylor it appeared that the lads, who had been work- ing all night, and were going home about six o'clock in the morning, were seen by Taylor to knock some coping stones off a wall which fenced a field.—They were each fined 15s. —Hunt's father asked if a receipt could be given to him after paying the money, ache intended taking further action in the matter, Ito being of opinion that Taylor had sworn falsely.—He was informed that action could be taken without a receipt. JUVENILE THIEVES —Walter Abbott (12) and Jas. Leahy (7) were charged with stealing cakes from the shop of Mr. Hose, confectioner, Church-street. Evidence was given by a boy who was set by the prisoners to watch while they carried off some eccles cakes from the shop.—Thos. Leahy (14) and John Keenan (11) were charged with stealing on Tuesday, the 16th, some cakes from the same shop.—After the parents of the boys had been cautioned, Thomas Leahy, who had been convicted of stealing previously, was sent to prison for fourteen days; and to a reformatory for 'four years. Abbott and Keenan WerS ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod; James Leahy, brother of Thomas, four strokes. Two PLUCKY YOUTHS.—Henry Holland (17) and Andrew Harman (16) were charged with stealing a basket contain- ing the plimks of four pigs, on Thursday, the 10th inst.— James Roughley, Peter-street, St. Helens, carter, said he was going along Chain-lane with the basket and its contents in a cart. The basket was safe on crossing the bridge, but 500 yards further on it had disappeared.—Edward Lawrenson said that be saw the prisoners take the basket, and he spoke to theni about it, saying to Holland, who actually took the basket, that he was a very foolish fellow, and told him to replace the basket. Holland replied that be was hungry, and was not going to "clem" as long as there was meat.— Prisoners pleaded guilty, and were each fined 10s. and costs, 215., or twenty days' imprisonment. AN INTOXICATED DEFENDANT.—CharIes Clisham, who appeared to have taken something stronger than water, was I charged with unlawfully assaulting Susannah Clisham, his I wife, on the 20th October.—Defenclant pleaded guilty.—Mr. R. W. IL Thomas, who appeared for prosecutrix, said defen- dant was a collier residing in Volunteer-street, and was a man of very violent character, especially when under the influence of drink. She lead been obliged on various occa- sions to leave him. On the 30th October he woke up early taenedths.truucke Li s nt wifehe m tonr n thein g , fgaoote some with e breakingto o a largeon e o f knife her also threatened to murder her. On the following Saturday s he struck her with a poker. They had been married seven years, and at the time of the assault were living in lodgings. At present she was living at Prescot with her sister.—While nrosecutrix was giving -her evidence defendant frequently interrupted the court, correcting the evidence by frequent interpolations which were accompanied by very choice lan- guage; and also blackening the character of his wife.—Thi Bench resolved not to proceed with the ease until the defen- lant had come to his senses.—On going downstairs he said he would "remember" his wife "for this."

Throughout Monday night and up to THE GREAT STOR,:Nni.advancedmostsevere hour on Tuesday morning a very violent gale raged over nearly thein UsnciotetdianKdi,n,g:hloeirne. and great deslruction of property wrought. Telegraphic several esreaelmisi vteos were lost and railway communication in that part of the country was to a large extent brought to a stoppage, and reports concur in showing that the storm was equal in intensity to that which swept down to Tay Bridge. Afire, which broke out in a house at Ayr, was so fanned by the high wind that 16 houses were destroyed, and 100 persons are consequently rendered homeless. On the coast there were numerous ship- wrecks, and the foundering of one vessel at Ardrossan was attended by the loss of seven lives. The storm was also severe on the Lancashire coast, and we have the customary accounts of flood and havoc at Blackpool.

TRADE NOTES. The factory of Messrs. Goodbody, at Clan, was on Tues- day closed. and the employee, numbering 600, were paid off. They hal struck for higher wages, but eventually consented to work on condition that their leaders were Teinstated. The employers declined, and closed the works. Fifteen hundred persons are dependant on the factory,

THE EX_ 4MI NER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 26, 1881. ST. HELENS POLICE COURT. !DEATH OF MR. W. E. WINSTANLEY, OF NEWTON, THE INQUEST. Mi. W. E. Winstanley, a well known member of the War- rington Board of Guardians, died suddenly on Saturday morning last, at his residence, High-street, Newton-le- Willows. Ou Thursday evening he retired to rest at seven o'clock, apparently in his usual health, and he made no com- plaint. About two o'clock next morning, be awoke in great agony, and Dr. Broe, who was called in, gave a prescription. During all Friday he continued in great pain, and in the evening Dr. Broe left half a dozen powders, each containing half a grain of opium, to be administered half hourly until the pain was alleviated. Three had been given the patient at nine o'clock, when the family retired to bed, leaving ties servant girl, 14 years of age, to wait on the patient. She administered another at 9-35, and by his orders went to bed at ten o'clock, putting the remaining powders on a small table within his reach. The servant went into the room the following morning at seven o'clock (Saturday), and found Mr. Winstanley breathing heavily. She informed Miss Winstanley, and inatructions were given not to disturb him. On going into the room again at eight o'clock, the servant found Mr. Winstanley was dead. Mr. Winstanley was 66 years of age. He was an active and efficient member of Newton Board of Commissioners for about 15 years, and was senior overseer for that township. For upwards of 20 years he was a member of Warrington Board of Guardians, having been elected in April, 1857. His knowledge of poor law administration was considerable, and his services to the Board received recognition in March, 1379, when he was appointed chairman. It was during his chairmanship, and partly through his strong advocacy, that it was decided to build the Padgate schools, which are now approaching com- pletion. All the public bodies with which Mr. Winstanley was connected received the benefit of his active inquiring spirit, all questions receiving his conscientious considera- tion. His business, we understand, will be carried on by his family. The interment took place on Tuesday afternoon, at St. Oswald's Catholic Church, Ashton-in-Makerfield. The funeral cortege, which consisted of eight mourning coaches, started from the residence of the deceased, and along the route taken to the burial ground the respect of the in- habitants was manifested by the closed shops, and the darkened houses. The coffin was borne to the grave by four of Mr. Winstanley's old workmen, who desired to pay this tribute to his memory. The service of the Catholic Church was read by the Bev. Father O'Reilly. The following is a list of the gentlemen who accompanied the funeral:— Mr. T. and Mr. W. E. Winstanley (sons of the deceased), Messrs. T. Hunt, R. Hunt, Knight, and Hughes (relatives), the Revs. J. Yonge and J. Allatt, Dr. Spinks, and Messrs. Joseph Harrison (Chairman of the Warrington Board of Guardians), E. C. Cooper, Blackhurst, W. Darbyshire, Greening, Balharry, J. Swinton, B. B. Glover, J. C. Sutton (Clerk to the Board of Guardians), F. Gooch (Chairman of the Newton Board of Commissioners), B. Brierley, G. Wood, T. Forster, R. Barton, J. Caldwell, J. Houghton, Garnett, Hawkins, H. Houghton, Ball, and Mines (Superintendent of the Workhouse Schools). Colonel McCorquodale, who was unable to attend the funeral, courteously placed his carriage at the disposal of Mr. Winstaney's family. Considering the circumstances under which Mr. Winstanley had died, the County Coroner deemed it ad- visable to hold an inquest, and Mr. Barker, his deputy, accordingly attended at Newton on Wednesday morning for that purpose. The first witness called was W. E. Winstanley, son of the deceased, who said his father had been in failing health, more or less, for sometime. At half-past one on Friday morning, he complained of a pain across the bowels, and witness went for the doctor. Dr. Broe prescribed for him. Deceased had been a drive with Mr. Wallington the night before. On Friday' evening witness went out at six o'clock and did not return until ten o'clock, and as his father was then sleeping nicely he did not go into his room. When he went to breakfast the follow- ing morning about half-past eight, his sister told him one of his father's hands was very cold and he seemed to be uncon- scious. He went into the room and saw his father was either dead or dying. Ile consequently ran for the doctor, who went immediately, and after examining him said it was "alt over." A juryman inquired if deceased had complained previously of illness, and witness said his father was told by a doctor a week or two ago that he might live for 20 years yet. Elizabeth Winstanley said her father had suffered all his life from indigestion and disease of the liver. About a month ago he consulted Dr. White, of Warrington, and had not been attended by a doctor since. On Thursday night he went to bed about seven o'clock, when he appeared in his usual health. He always retired to bed early, sometimes at six o'clock. He called the servant girl up at 1.30 on Friday morning, and she told witness that master said he was dying. He was very nervous and always said that when he was ill. She went into his room and reassured him. He said be had a severe pain in his stomach, and she at once sent for a doctor. Dr. Broe went, and gave him some medicine, telling witness she might give him a little brandy and water. She stopped up with him all that night, and at nine o'clock she sent for Dr. Watkins agiin. He prescribed a warm bath, and then to apply warm moist cloths to his stomach. She gathered from the doctor's manner that there was nothing alarming in her father's condition. The doc'or called again at half past eleven and said her father was much better. Her father asked how long a person suffering like that could live, and the doctor said he would pull him through. He was in continuous pain. The doctor left some pills, ef which she gave her father three at the stated times. At her father's request she again sent for the dant* and Dr. Bros gave her the mann, etg /Iv trimi.nigtsal; eecond at 8-30, the mina at 9-5, and the fourth was given by the servant at 9-35. The girl at his request left him alone at ten o'clock. Witness awoke about seven o'clock on Saturday morning, and the servant told her deceased was asleep. She told her not to diatorb him. The servant again went into the room about eight o'clock, and returned saying he looked funny and had one eye open. Witness went into the room, but did not think he was dead. She told her brother, who after seeing deceased said "It's all over." She did not believe him and sent for a doctor, who, however, said be was quite dead. Mr. Houghton: Did you think this servant capable of ad- ministering the medicine and taking charge of your father? —Most certainly. She was accustomed to be with him; and if I had been dying I could have trusted her. I should not have left her but I thought my father would go to sleep. Mary Silverburn said she had been the general servant for the deceased for fifteen months, and during that period he had been generally ill. She had waited upon him. He called her up about 12-30 on Friday morning, and said lie had ,felt poorly at seven o'clock but had not mentioned it. He seemed to be in great pain, and she lit the fire and warmed him some plates which he placed on his stomach. She remained up all night with him and Miss Winstanley from about three o'clock. She gave the same account as the last witness as to the visits and instructions of the doctor, also with regard to administering the powders. At nine o'clock the family went to bed, and Mr. Winstanley told her to go at ten o'clock which she did. She heard no dis- turbance during the night. A few minutes past seven o'clock on Saturday morning, she entered the room of deceased, who was breathing very heavily as if he had got a bad cold. She informed Miss Winstanley, who told her not to make a noise as she might waken him. Again at eight she went to look at him and he appeared very strange. He had one eye open. She informed Miss Winstanley and subsequently the doctor was called in. The powder packets were in exactly the same place where she had placed them, but the deceased had taken the contents of one. J. J. Broe, M.R.C.S., Edinburgh, assistant to Dr. Watkins, attributed death to a hepatic colic shock and failure of the heart. When he visited deceased on Friday morning he was iu great pain and extremely exhausted. A gall stone was passing through the gallduct, and the pain was "killing" if not quickly relieved. He gave six powders in the evening to be taken half hourly. Ile composed them himself and they contained half a grain of opium each. That was simply a narcotic. Dr. Watkin called between ten and eleven o'clock on Friday night but was not heard. Any man could have swallowed all the six powders at once and not been affected. In summing up, the Coroner said the jury must dismiss any rumours they had heard outside, and only consider the evidence. Under the circumstances there was only one ver- dict they conld give—natural causes, but if they were not satisfied there was only one cause open and that was to have the body exhumed, and the contents of the atom ich analysed. The servant girl had given her evidence in an admirable way, and seemed to have attended to the deceased. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that death re- 'suited from natural causes.

MANCHESTER CORN, THURSDAY.—A very limited business has transpired during the week at drooping prices for every- thing except maize, which has commanded full rates. The mild and unseasonable weather has continued. Imports have been larger of wheat, flour, and peas, but only moderate of maze and other grain. The trade this morning was restricted to the supply of needy buyers. All but the finest samples r f English wheat was difficult to quote at lower prices. Foreign was purchasable at a t eduction of id. per cents'. Flour also tended in buyers' favour. Oats and oatmeal sold slowly, at barely former ouotat ions. Beans and peas were-dull. Maize was taken in retail at the full currencies of last market day. An inquest was held on Friday, by Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, on the body of the Rev. Father Sebastian Enrico, passionist priest of the Sutton Monastery, who was killed in a shocking manner en the London and North Western Railway, at St. Helens Junction, on Wednesday, the leth inst. Mr. Ferrand appeared for the railway company. The Rev. Father Basil Moubart, vice-rector of the Passionist Monastery, Sutton, said he had seen the remains, and bad no doubt they were those of a priest, who was known as the Rev. Sebastian Enrico. He was 54 years of age, and an Italian by birth, but had lived for N years in France. About twelve months ago he was expelled, and had since been in Rome and London without a charge, until three months since he came to the Sutton monastery. On Wednesday morning he said he was going out, but did not say where to. About twenty minutes to eleven, witness was told the accident had occurred and went to the station. He was of opinion that deceased saw the train coming up and was so anxious to get in that he did not think of his ticket. Wit- ness was of opinion that deceased could not understand what the porter said, as it was hard to make him understand Eng- lish. He had not the slightest suspicion that deceased in- tended suicide, but he had that morning complained of dizziness in the head, and had been under Dr. Donnellan.— The Doctor said he had experienced great difficulty in mak- ing deceased understand, and had to use Latin phrases to do so. Unless the porter accompanied his commands with gestures, deceased might have thought it meant to call him on.—Thomas Archer, porter, said about twenty-three mi rill tes past ten on Wednesday morning deceased came to the edge of the up platform and asked if that was the train for Liver- pool. The train from:Manchester was just drawing up to the platform, and an express was coming from Liverpool. Witness shouted "Stand back, stand back," and immediately the trains crossed. He beard the whistles of the express, and directly afterwards saw deceased rolling underneath the train. Deceased was cut to pieces, the face and part of the head being completely knocked away. His body was .fear- fully mangled and was collected and placed in a sheet. Witness had never seen a body so terribly mutilated before.— idmund ‘Vhitehead, driver of the express, said he was run- ning at about N miles an hour. On nearing the junction station he saw deceased on the platform and said to his mate. "That man is going to jump off; we are going to kill him." He jumped off and stood in the middle of the road, and did not stir a foot, he seeming as if lie was fast to the ground. The whistles were blown, but they could not stop, and , deceased was knocked down and killed.—Dr. Donnellan suggested that someone should be there to prevent people crossing over the level. The Coroner said the company had entirely remodelled the station within the last two or three years, and every pre- caution seemed to have been taken.—The jury returned a verdict cf "Accidental death."

div.head: GRAND CONCERT AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: GRAND CONCERT AT ST. HELENS.

The St. Helens Congregational Church Choir gave their fifth annual concert on Monday evening, under the patron- age of His Worship the Mayor (Mr. Richard Pilkington), in the Assembly Room, Brook-street. There was a good atten- dance. The principal artistes were Miss Laura Smart, soprano; Miss Sharpies, mezzo soprano; Mr. George Barton, tenor ; Mr. Henry Parr, baritone ; and Mr. Fred Gordon, basso. There was also a band and chorus of about 70 per- formers, under the conductorship of Mr. T. T. Elliot. Miss Emily Gardner presided at the pianoforte, and Mr. Jahn Hayes at the American organ. The music was efficiently performed, and a rare musical treat was enjoyed. The first part of the evening's entertainment opened with selections from Handers great oratorio "Israel in Egypt." The piece Opened with a recitative by Mr. Barton, descriptive of the bondage of Israel in Egypt and the mission of Moses who worked signs and wonders amongst them. The chorus which followed, showing how God sent a thick darkness over the land, was rendered man appropriately solemn manner. Miss Smart and Miss Hewitt joined in the duet "The Lord is my strength and my song, He is become my salvation," but if a little more distinct articulation and energy had been thrown into the piece by the latter lady, it would have been much more enjoyable. Mr. Barton received the applause of the audience in his rendering of the air which describes the threatenings of Pharoah and his host, after the Children of Israel had fled from their captivity. This was followed by the recitative and air by Mr. Fred Gordon. whose robust bass voice and dramatic power did full justice to the passage, in which was described the drowning of the pursuers of the , Israelites in the Red Sea. The chorus, " Thy right hand 0 1 Lord, hath dashed in pieces the enemy" was effectively ' rendered, and received the hearty plaudits of the audience. The efforts of Messrs. Gordon and Parr in the passage com- mencing "The Lord is a man of war, Lord is His name," re- ceived the appreciation of the audience who demanded a repetition, which was given. Miss Smart again followed, and the piece was concluded in a spirited manner by the render- 1 ing of the chorus," The horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea." An adaption of Coleridge's celebrated poem "The Ancient Mariner," formed the second part of the pro- gramme. The pith of this story is that Living shot an albatross, the ancient mariner and his companions were sub- jected to fearful penalties. The ancient mariner sorely repented the cruel work of his cross-bow. He was forgiven, and on reaching land he told his story to a hermit. Through distress of mind he was driven from land to land, and where- gar Pre swriatu itie at Ziel iswtellle theilait7nYiCil. meR ttiaig tette by Misses Sharpies a-d Smith, Messrs. Berry and Parr, was comprised in the cantata, the chorus to which "0 happy, happy living things, no tongue their beauty might declare," was well rendered. Miss Smart followed with the passage commencing "0 sleep it is a gentle thing," accompanied by a soprano chorus which was especially pleasing. Messrs. , Gordon and Barton executed their recitations and airs in admirable style. Miss Smart and Miss Parryareceived quite 1 an ovation at the finish of their duet, in which their voices blended admirably. The piece was well sung, the only thing to complain of being the transposition of words by Miss Smart, and the introduction of others foreign to the poem. To the uninitiated who were trying to follow the piece with- out the very necessary adjunct to a performance of this sort, the "book of words," this neglect of the IP ecise language of the piece would not convey an intelligible meaning to their minds. The concert, from a musical point of view, was, however a success, which mast have highly gratified Mr. Elliott, whose efforts to educate the people to an appreciation of the higher class music, deserve the encouragement of all. The chorus consisted of singers of several choirs in the neighbourhood, and included most of the members of the Albion Glee Union.
