div.p: PIIESENT.ATION IN THE VIO'fORIA • HALL. ST. HELENS. The fourth anniversary of the Rev. Mr. Green's ministry in this hall was observed on Sunday and Monday last. Good congregations assembled all day on Sunday, the at- tendance being taken as 100 on the Sunday morning, and 230 in the evening. Collections were made at both these services, amounting to £3 10s., on behalf of the work. The Rev. Mr. Green pretched throughout the day. On Monday evening the proceedings commenced by a tea meeting for the friends. The tea was announced for six o'clock, but long before that time the hall was filled, and at the an- nounced time was packed, amongst those present being S. J. Menzies, Esq. (Liverpool), the Rev. C. Green and Mr . Green, and Mr. Barker (St. Helens). It was estimated that not less than 500 sat down to a good and snbstantial tea, there being two sittings. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mesdames Ellard, Barber, Davies, Green, Appleton, Lucas, Groves, Miss Wycherly, Houghton, and others. After tea a public 'meeting was held, and every available seat was occupied; about 600 were pressed. Mr. S. J. Menzies, of Liverpool, who, we may say, is the founder of the hall, and by whose generosity the church is largely maintained, received an enthusiastic reception, his kindness evidently being appreciated by the vast number present. Earnest addresses were delivered by Mr. A. Brown (Liverpool), Mr. W. Brown (Manchester), Mr. B. F. Babcock (West Derby), and Mr. Thomas Lydiatt (of Birkenhead). The addresses, which referred to Mr. Green's work, were at- tentively listened to. One pleasing feature in the proceed- ings was a presentation to the pastor and his wife; the latter of whom we may say is also an earnest worker in conjunction with her husband. The presentation to Mrs. Green consisted of a handsome framed picture, a bold land- scape, and to Mr. Green a Biblical Commentary. These were subscribed for and purchased by friends at Eccleston Hill Mission Room, the lady who had specially exerted her- self in procuring the gifts being Mrs. John Jones, of Eccleston Hill. We may mention that the subscriptions emanated from those friends who had profited by the work and ministry of the pastor of the hall and his devoted wife, and as a token of the high esteeem in which they were held by their friends the presentation was made. The presenta- tion was made by Mr. Menzies; and in conclusion we may add that the labours of Mr. and Mrs. Green have rildently not been in vain, and we trustthat increasing bleP,in, may rest upon the good works they are doing in the n; ;Ebour- hood.

Darn CONGREGATIONAL BAND or HOPE.—Tho firs. meeting in connection with this society was held on Mon day last. The chair was taken by Mr. Dan Boyd, and over 300 persons were present. Songs, recitations, readitags, Arc., were given by the members, assisted by Miss Hankieson, of Thelwall, who gave 2 solos in an excellent manner, and they were well received. The speaker was the Rev. DISTRICT NEWS. POLICE INSPECTION AT PRESCOT.—On Tuesday fore. noon, Captain Alinson inspected the Prescot Division of the Lancashire County Constabulary in the court yard adjoin- ing the Police Station, Derby-street. There were on parade one superintendent (Mr. Barker), two inspectors (Messrs. Barnett and Mahoe), seven sergeants, and 58 constables, total 68; the remainder of the force being left on duty. The inspector afterwards examined the books, clothing, and accoutrements of the men, the building,&c., with the condi- tion of which he seemed perfectly satisfied. PROPOSED PRESENTATION TO CAPTAIN CROSS, OP PRESCOT.—It is pleasing to notice that a subscription has been set on foot among the non-commissioned officers and men of the late 48th (Prescot) L.R.V. (now forming K Company of the 21st L R.V.), for the purpose of making a presentation to Captain Cross, whe has been identified with the volunteer movement in Prescot a good many years, as a token of their esteem and good will. The present, it is stated, will take the form of a elver cream jug, sugar basin, and tongs in morocco case, and the ceremony of handing . over the same to the gallant captain will take place at an , early date. cr Sr. ao.ELENS STARR-BOWE/ITT BIJILDING &Misty,— The fourteenth appropriation of the Ist St. Helens (284)* Starr.Bowkett Building Society was made in the tarp room of the Cocoa Rooms, Market-place, on Tuesday evening last, Mr. G. Barrow in the chair. The scrutineers appointed to conduct the balloting were Messrs. J. Loader and R. W. Daft. The ballot resulted in No. 441 being drawn, when, after a resolution had been passed confirming the ballot, Mrs. Jane Marsh, of Parr Stocks, wife of a collier, was declared entitled to the appropriation, she being the holder of register No. 441. The amount of the appropriation was £206, making altogether f.. 3,000 that has been appropriated, by ballot, free of interest to the members of this society. Paxecor Wonsasha Mares Isreneveg. The first entertainment of the season, in connection with the Prescott Working Men's Society, took place, on Thursday, in thew Assembly-rooms, Derby-street. The chair was occupied by') Mr. John Johnson Brown, and there was a very largf audience. The Chairman, in the cowed Of a brief speecK referred to the formation of the societr' in_ 1868, and ob- served that those present knew pretty well what it hair accomplished in that period in the way of 'previding soma and wholesome reading, a variety of gamea and other attrac- tions whereby young men had been prevented from go to, encored for her efficient rendering fo' the song above meae I tioned. The band was also successful lii seouripg an encore.' Owing to the indisposition of Miss Quick, Afi..W. H. Read; of Woolton, performed the arduous duties of accompanist. The second part of the p -ogramme was acomedy in two acts, entitled "Never be inquisitive," by the Prescot Amateurs, the dramatis persona being as follows:—Paul Pry, Mr. J. Sinnott; Captain Haselton, Mr. J. Lewis; Mr. Oldbutton, Mr. W. Jackson • Sir Spangle Rainbow, Mr.l. Hignett ; Porn- made (hie valet), Mr. R. Cox; tankard (the landlord), Mr. W. Braithwaite; Billy fa waiter), Mr. P. Lightfoot; Tommy (a servant), Mr. W. Meredith; Laura (old button's ward); Miss Pye ; Crump (her maid), Miss Lawrenson. The whole of the characters were well potutrayed, and it would there- fore be invidious to particularise. The costumes were ap- propriate, and there was a marked improvement in the size of the stage. The scene painting, which comprised a well known street and hotel in Prescot, Derby-street and the "Royal," was performed by Mr. Isaac Hignett in his spa re time and he deserves infinite for the excellent manner in which he has executed the work. A word of praise is also due to the secretary of the committee, Mr. P. Lightfoot, who has been indefatigable in his endeavours to provide the public of Prescot with a pleasant evening. At the close, the chair- man announced that the comedy would be again given next Monday evening. The proceeds would be handed over to Mrs. W. S. Evans towards the maintenance of the towo nurse. Mr. A. Perris read a paper, before the members of thie .I!tociety, on Wedoesday-evening, entitled f: Elianbeth Harrett ..A. • • - .orotiiiing; our ' greatest woman-poet." Theryasionly a scanty attendance, and Dr. C. White presided. Tieerlacturer, after speaking of idealization and expression, a*4 he held Mrs. Browning to be our greatest woman poet.!..There were qualities in her poems which admitted of comparison with those of the greatest men. She bad the breadth and versa- linty of a man ; no sameness; no one idea; no type character; our single Shakesperean woman: Of her early 'poems, " The drama of life " 3orresponded in subject to 'Milton's "Paradise Lost," and the "Seraphim "to "Paradise 'Regained," but they could not bear any comparison as fat As literary ability was concerned to the works of the great Puritan poet. The language was the weakest part of Mrs. Browning's early poems. The diction was rugged, the Imagery often borders on the grotesque. we were always conscious of more or less extravagance and obscurity. But ' these poems, in spite of their many defects, announced that 'another great poet in the person of Elizabeth Barrett (not yet Mrs. Browning) had arisen in England, a poet of almost excessive fervour and intensity, whose imagination would quail before nothing in heaven, earth, or hell, and who pos- sessed at the same time the deepest tenderness that could dwell in a woman's heart. Putting aside Dante and Milton, he knew nothing in religious poetry at all comparable for imaginative power with the drama of Earle and The Seraphim. The imagery of these poems, especially of the former was so vaguely gorgeous that many readers would be permanently repelled by them. They bore throughout the impress of an original mind and a sovereign imagination, and the deep beating of a woman's heart made fine sweet music in them from first to last. Amid the stormy grandeurs of their imagery this deep music came in with enhanced effect as the penetrating tenderness of " Home, sweet home" might come in amid the melodious crash of orchestral thunderings. ( Applause.) As we proceeded in our examination of Mrs. Browning's poems we found them becoming more human in subject and more simple in treatment. He compared "The poet's vow" to Tennyson's "Elaine," and described "Isabel's child," giving quotations. He criticised her "Lady Geraldine's courtship," which he said belonged to the SAMS class of poems as Tennyson's " Locksley Hall." In her shorter poems we perpetually came upon lines and stanzas imbued with that domestic sentiment, that home- bred feeling, at which some sneered, but of which others were justly proud as a characteristic of English society. It was in the sincerity of her heart that she asked— What music certes can you find As soft as voices which are kind" The lecturer th n recited "The sleep," and interestingly described "Aurora Leigh," from which he largely quoted, and concluded by saying that Mrs. Browning had exalted her sex. (Applause.) Mr. EIRCIIALL, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Perris, remarked that his extracts had been exceedingly beautiful, and would make them desire to know more of a poetess who seemed to be so worthy to be known. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. R. PILCHER, 8.A., said it had given him im- mense pleasure to listen to the paper. It was so many years since he had read "Aurora Leigh" that it had been a real pleasure to have his memory refreshed. He was exceedingly struck with the truth so well brought out by Mr. Perris that a poet was a creator, and when they thought that imagina- tion was the living link between the intellect and the con- science, and that where imagination was deficient, as in ignorant, brutalised people, or people in a low grade of development, such as savages, that cruelty was their charac- teristic which he attributed to the fact that the imaginative power of putting one's-self in another's pl ice was defective, they would thus see how important it was that the poets, creators, or seers of our race should be more studied—(hear, hear,)—and made more use of in education. He very cor- dially seconded the proposition. Mr. Tuttxxn and the CHAIRMAN having supported the proposition, which was carried, Mr. FERRIS expressed his thanks. The proceedings then terminated.

- SUICIDE.—On Wednesday morning the body of a man named Wilson was taken out of the Mere. He had sent a letter to Mr. Unsworth, in Mill-lane, near to where he lived, informing him that his body would be found in a certain part of the lake. Some alleged difference with members of •kis family had led him to commit the crime of destroying himself. The body awaits an inquest at the nearest public. house.

- --•-- DRINKING FouNTA.IN.—By the kindness of J. D. Kay Esq., J.p., of Winsford Lodge, a drinking fountain has been erected in the Market Place, which will prove not only an ornament but really useful. To a large extent the town of Winsford has been getting gradually one necessity after another supplied. Improvements have only taken place when their stern necessity was demonstrated to the Local Board, But it is a matter of rejoicing that any private inhabitant is willing to come forward and add to the public convenience, or ornament of the hitherto little ornamented town of Winsford. This fountain is surmounted by a lamp, likewise the gift of one of the members of the Local Board (Mr. Jabez Hulse). We trust the example sA v ill be followed in other directions, until what was 0,, • a dark, unadorned town, may become as moderniz ‘s most around us.

REviver, SERYICES.—That a series of regul..r revival services are being held in the various chapels of Winsford, is not altogether attributable to the presence of the Salvation Army and their officers; but no casual observer even will deny that as those agents have been more or less so actively employed here some months now, that their influence is felt. Many who have long been absent from any place of worship have been, by their influence, drawn into serious ways. Some whose chief Sunday occupation seeped to be rabbit and dog coursing, racing, &c., changed their course of life for the better.

this Government is taking as much out of the people in taxes as the last, these Conservative special - pleaders feel they are treading upon dangerous ground; for they cannot but feel that the country sees through the subterfuge, and is fully aware that the Liberal Government has only been obliged to keep up the public income till now, because it has had to pay millions upon millions of Tory debts accumulated and left standing over when the men who contracted them were shifted out of place, and that as soon as ever these floating debts of the !Tend- thrift Tories are wiped out, the reduction of taxation may be expected to commence, which will confound their charges of high expenditure against a Liberal Administration. In these various parts of their policy and anagement of the nation's concerns, Mr. Gladstone and his mcol- leagues may defy their Tory assailants to impair the position they hold before the country. The contrast in all these respects is too great between Liberal and Tory government, and is too decisively in favour of Liberal rule. Well may the Conservative leaders fix upon Irish administration as the question upon which alone they can hope to pierce the defensive lines of the Ministry. But even there, is it not apparent that the Parnellite section of Irish revolutionists are abso- lutely the only recruits the Tory mongers have yet 'laid hold of ? What can the Government adversaries say about its system of governing Ireland? The most they can say is, in effect, what Sir Richard Cross has said this week, that Liberal Governments try to keep Irishmen in order by offering them the broadest measures of protection for their industrial interests compatible with equity, which they can pass through Parliament ; and by ruling them as long as ever they can upon the same constitutional principles as Englishmen and Scotchmen are governed under. This, the Tories declare, is a flagrant blunder of Liberal Irish policy—to treat Irishmen as if they were men, and were capable of being moulded by liberal treat- ment into loyal and law-abiding subjects. Irishmen, say the Tories, can be managed only as we have always managed them—as mere undisciplined, way- ward, refractory children, to be kept sternly under restraint, and forbidden any of those rights and powers of self •government which are only fit for races which have advanced to the stage of mature manhood. Sir Richard Cross impugns Mr. Glad- stone's method with disaffected Irishmen as altogether too indulgent. Well, ills about the one point of all Tory contention as to which there may be some slight show of reason in their view, having regard to the circumstances of the position. What we mean to say is, that the conduct of some Irishmen during the last twelve months, who have abused the liberty of action they were permitted to enjoy for a long time under Liberal administration, has no doubt been such as to afford a certain basis to the insistance of Conser- vatives that such men are not fit for perfect freedom, and not safe except when under the curb of an imperial authority. The Conservatives are entitled to bold that irreconcilable anarchists in Ireland can , never be restrained from fatal mischief without some permanent curtailment of their personal liberty. But when they would go on to apply this policy of repres- sion to the whole Irish people, English Liberals will still interpose firmly, and will earnestly insist that the question is still one to be decided, after a sufficient period of fair and deliberate trial, whether the main body of the inhabitants of Ireland can subsist in peaceful subjection and loyal obedience to established authority, under laws which, whilst they prevent or punish rapine and outrage, at the same time afford to those who submit to them the amplest protection against injustice by a dominant class.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

A complaint was made at the last meeting of the Prescot School Board that Mr. Lightfoot, the head schoolmaster, had been calling a boy by the nickname oi "Young Zulu," the result of which has been that lads in the streets have also applied the epithet to the boy. Mr. Lightfoot admits that he did use the epithet, although he says it was only whilst "he and the boys were having a bit of fun in the school- yard." One would imagine that a public schoolmaster ought to be above that sort of thing, because be is expected to be an example to his pupils, and if he uses such an epithet, even if it be "only in fun," how can he teach his scholars not to call other people by nicknames? Moreover, it should not be forgotten by schoolmasters that little boys, mischievous though they may be, have their tender feelings as well as other people, and those tender feelings should not be trampled upon, least of all by those whose business it is to be a pattern to others. It is the duty of school teachers to train up the children entrusted to their charge in the golden rule that they should "do unto others as they would that others should do unto them," and as I presume Mr. Lightfoot would not like rude epithets to be applied to him or his children, he should not apply them to little boys. Considerable discussion has been caused in tradesmen's circles in Runcorn in respect to the manner in which the contracts were given for blankets, at the last meeting of the Board of Guardians. It is alleged that the contract was awarded to the gentleman who charged the highest price, though the blankets were exactly the same, and made by the same manufacturer. There is an old saying to the effect that "kissing goes by favour," and in this particular instance it is alleged that the successful man won the palm because he was a young tradesman, and ought to have a little en- couragement. Shall I add that a number of Runcornians say that he carried off the contract not because of these reasons, but owing to being a Wesleyan Methodist. At first glance, there would not appear to be a very intimate rela- tionship between blankets and class meetings, but those who can "read between the lines" will probably be able to ex- plain the riddle. At any rate, when the poor paupers are kept at such a low figure, according to returns lately pre- sented to the Board, it is not the proper thing that the rate- payers' pockets should be touched for the purpose of benefitting any tradesman, and I hope for the credit of the Guardians concerned there is no foundation for so serious a charge. Whether Mr. Philip Speakman is under the impression that he does not get sufficient opportunities far airing his eloquence at the meetings of the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, or not, I cannot say; but most certainly he seems to have a Weakness for calling the members together on frivolous pretexts. What necessity there was for holdirg the special meeting of the Board which took place the other Friday evening must remain one of those enigmas which "no fellah can understand; " and there is a generally ex- pressed wish amongst Mr. Speakman's fellow members that he may be led to read Foster's essay on "The improvement of time," or some of the philosopher Franklin's productions, and not in future be the cause of so much waste in the • matter of time, which one of our great writers says is than , geld more sacred, and to a certain class of persons, in which I should be the last person in the world to include Mr. Philip, "like lead."

The advent of the Rev. George Hack into the Runcorn Wes- leyan Methodist circuit, seems to have acted like "new blood" in more secular associations. Whatever any "car- ping critic" may be inclined to say against the new minister he will not be enabled to allege that he is wanting in enthu- siasm, and there was never anything great or good done in this world without the possession of this faculty in a con- siderable degree. Special efforts are now being made, under the direction of the Superintendent (Mr. Nowell) to make of use the splendid machinery possessed by the Wesleyan Methoclists of Runcorn for the carrying on of spiritual cork. I have long been of the same opinion as the Rev. Dr. Parker, of the City Temple, London, that far too little use is made by the various sects of the magnilicent and costly buildings possessed by them. Why should they be closed most of the week instead of being utilised for various good purposes ? In ' the golden age, which seems to be as yet, a very long way gofisthtoe Chanyaetourpon lint wt the er d us wn ilti ei cdhssthaat el ls sesinl acpt ieflys ito fft'oevthe er yut !lei sn 1 are used for a variety of good purposes during the week and it is a matter of regret that such beautiful structures as St. Paul's, and Halton-road churches should not be made mere useful. There are cities on the continent where l Roman Catholic places of worship are always open.

On Thursday °ming a dramatic performance in aid of the Railway Benevolent In.titution, will be given in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes, under distinguished patronage. From what I know of some of the gentlemen who have the matter in hand, I feel confident the arrangements will be admirably carried out.

I hear that Mr. Pierpoint, of Runcorn, sang the other day at the Lord Mayor's banquet, and that a notice appeared in the Times. Judging from Mr. Pierpoint's singing at the Madrigal Society's concert, there is no doubt that he wit in a very short time, take his place amongst the leading vocalists of the day

Dlscotrusz ox Tux PRINCE or Deamates.—The Rev. T. A. Carver, the pastor of the Baptist chapel, Hutchinson - street, Widnes, is aow preaching a series of sermons. The discourse on Sunday was on "A checked devil." WIDNEs Psuisn Cuuncu.—The Rev. Septimus Hutchinson preached three times at the Widnes Parish Church, on Sunday, on behalf of the Church Missionary

Society. ACCIDENT AT TEE OLD QUAY WORKS, RIINCORN.—On Saturday, a young man named William Lewis was slightly scalded is the face, whilst employed at Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele's works, Runcorn. He was attended by

Dr. Mouritz. A RUNCORN Titer ACCIDENT.—On Monday, as Edward Jackson, painter, Blantyre-street, Runcorn, was riding:along Church-street, in that town, in a trap belonging to Mr. Sexton, of Northwich, and near the National Schools, the wheels of the vehicle caught against the kerbstone, and Jackson was thrown out. He was rendered insensible, and taken to the surgery of Dr. Robinson, where his rather serious injuries were attended to. HALTON PARISH CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—An essay, entitled "The moral and social con- ditions of the working classes," was given by Mr. C. W. Brown, in the girls' schoolroom, Halton, in connection with the above society, on Tuesday evening. In the absence of his brother, Mr. Daniel Baguley occupied the chair, and there were 42 members present. After the essayist had read his paper, a discussion was opened, in which the following gentlemen took path—The Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. .1. Wright, R. Sandy, D. Baguley, F. Thomason, R. Hughes,B. Haddock, and W. Hughes. A vote of thanks to the essayist was proposed by Mr. T. Wright, and seconded by Mr. J. Han- cock, for the splendid entertainment he had afforded them. Mr. Sandy proposed, and Mr. W. Hughes seconded, the motion that the thanks of this meeting be also accorded to Mr. Baguley for taking the chair. WIDNES PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS ENTERTAINMENT. The third of the series of entertainments which are being field during the present winter at the above schools, in aid of the Class Room Funds, took place on Tuesday evening. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided, and in his opening ad- dress alluded to the excellent style in which the Glee Class went through their pieces, which he thought very creditable to them—The Glee Class gave the pieces, "The stars that above us are shining," " Let the hills resound with song," and "hence, now, away," with their customary correctness and spirit. Miss 'Alice Purver's song, "Home they brought her warrior dead," was given with pathos and expression, and obtained an encore. Mr. F. W. Wilkinson's song, "Sailing," was also encored; and Mr. W. Thomas' song, "The agony column," met with an equally hearty reception. In her second song, "My home's in the valley," Miss Alice Purver scored a success equal to that which bad marked her previous effort. Mr. J. Forster gave to readings, which were exceptionally good, and, being of a humorous nature, tickled the risible faculties of the audience in no small degree. Mr. Stirrup and Mr. W. M. Brown (of the School for the Blind, Hardman-street, Liverpool) gave duets and solos on the pianoforte in a very successful manner, and were encored on each occasion.

COLLISION BETWEEN FERRY STEAMERS AND FLATS ON THE RIVER MERSEY.—On the 18th inst., in the Liverpool County Court, before Mr. T. Perronet Thompson, judge, and Captain Lott and Captain Homewood, nautical assessor, the two eaSea of Whitehead v. the Corporation of Birkenhead, and Austin v. the Corporation of Birkenhead, came on for trial.—Mr. W. J. Stewart, barrister, instructed by Mr. J. W. Thompson, appeared on behalf of the plaintiffs in each action, and Mr. T. 11. James, barrister, instructed by the Town Clerk of Birkenhead, appeared for the defendants.— The plaintiffs claimed.dainages far injury sustained by their flats (the "Intrepid" and the ‘• Lousia ") by collision with the ferry steamer " Birkenhead," in the river Mersey, oia the Bth September. Both cases were by consent tried together. From the evidence it appeared that the two flats were at the time of the collision in tow of the Weston Point screw tug " Liberator," on their way from Weston Point to Liverpool. When nearing the south end of the George'a landing stage, the ferry steamer was seen to leave the stage, and although every effort was made by the tug and flats to keep out of the way, the ferry steamer kept on her course, eventually obliging the tug steamer to shift the towropes, and causing the two flats to strike the :erry steamer on her port side, doing her no damage but causing the fl its a considerable amount of damage—The Court was of opinion, on the evi- dence, that the ferry steamer was entirely to blame for not having seen the tug and fists before it became too late to avoid a collision, and directed judgment too be en- tered for the plaintiffs in the first case for £47 lie. 10d., and in the second for £lB 2s. 6d., with costs in each OPENING OF THE NEW CATHOLIC SCHOOLS AT WIDNES. —The Catholics of St. Mary's, at Widnes, have just erected a beautiful new school, which will afford accommodation for 600 children, at a cost of about £1,300; and on MuriPay evening, a tea party and concert were held for the purpose of celebrating the opening. The trays were given by Mesdames Pierce Tallon, Joha 'Fallon, Anderson, Edward Gould, Davis Gould Tayleton, Hewitt, and Newton, Hoyle, and Misses Jameson, and Moran. About 2,000 people were present. After-tea, the chair was taken by Dr. O'Keeffe, who previous to the commencement of the concert, said a few' words as to the aim of the gathering. Their object was for the advancement of education on behalf of the new schools,l which bad just been completed, and which would in a few I days be opened. The result of the recent examination was satisfactory, and they had obtained a very favourable report. The school, he may say, had done the best in the district. (Applause.) An interesting programme was then gone torough, and during the musical part of the proceedings Miss Cullen acted as accompanist. The comic song "When Ireland is free," was given with much spirit by Messrs. T. Mulvaney, and T. Stoner. Miss M. Johnson sang the song "Killarney," with great sweetness and expression, and was applauded. Miss Johnson, of Simms-cross, sang in capital ttyle "The last rose of summer," "Kathleen Mavourneen," was very prettily sung by Miss Hewitt, and Messrs. Mul- v.sney, and Storer gave a laughable sketch. The entire pro- Lecdings passed off very pleasantly. RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—At the weekly meeting of this society, held on Tuesday, three new members were introduced to the speaker.—The Home S-cretary, in introducing his bill called the "Removal of Parliamentary Disabilities Bill," made a very neat and effective speech, which apparently met with the hearty approval of the majority on the Government •side of the House.—The member for Winchester, in opposing the mea- sure, referred to the recent struggles which had taken place between the members of the House of Commons and Mr. Bradlaugh on his approaching the table of that House. It reminded him of the phrase "peace at any price." It was ridiculous to think that because one man out of 656 would not conform to the laws of the constitution, they were to alter the whole constitution. The constitution w s founded on the belief in a "Supreme Being," and the Bible was His • revelation. He argued that any man who would not submit to the acknowledgtnont of a God was unfit to sit in the British House of Commons.—The Indian Secretary believed if it had not been for Mr. Bradlaugh's proposed attack on the perpetual pension, he would have been allowed to sit in the House of Commons, but the Conservative party knew there was a rod in pickle for them. The present bill was based upon a desire to give fair play to every man.—The member for l'reston thought there were laws affecting the country which required redress before the supposed grievances of a pr'vate individual, and he called the atten- tion of Her Majesty's Government to the serious responsi- bility they were incurring in altering a law which, be said, would seriously affect the future welfare of this country. Ile wished to know what the Government meant by endea- vouring to admit a man whose interests were diametrically opposed to those of the country.—The member for Sand- wich strongly opposed the measure, and said he firmly believed that all nations grew and prosper d in accordance with their reverence to their Creator. If the present bill were passed, he (the speaker) thought it would be a step towards the final overthrow of this mighty empire. He begged to move its entire rejection, and also that the bill be read a second time that day six months.—The House then rose.—The member for Birkenhead gave notice that he would ask if her Majesty's Government had opened nego- tiations for the restoration of Cetewayo as King of Zululand, and if they had, to state the nature of them. FUNERAL OF A RuNconzr MUSIC TEACHER. Mr. Henry Jukes, who has for some time led a nomadic kind of life, and was a few weeks ago brought from a place north of England to his wife's house at Runcorn, in a very weak state, died there on the 12th inst., at the age of 55 years, after only being at home a very short time. Deceased was well known in Northwich as a music teacher of considerable ability; and many of his former friendeand pupils wishing to pay a tribute to his memory, it was decided that a pub- lic funeral should take place at Witton Church on Saturday afternoon. The body was taken in a hearse from Runcorn, and at the top of Winnington Hill was met by the bands of the Northwich and Hartford Volunteers, who were joined by several old pupils of the deceased, and a number of the in- habitants. Shortly after ten o'clock, the cortfige moved off, being led by the united bands playing the "Dead March." The hearse came next, and then a motaning coach, contain- ing Mrs. Jukes, Miss Mary Jukes, Miss Rose Jukes, Mr. T. B. Jukes, and Mr. S. Jukes—the widow and children of the deceased. A number of gentlemen—acquaintances of the late Mr. Jukes while he resided at Northwich—followed on , foot. As the body was being carried into the church, Mr. Pattison, the organist, played "I know that my Redeemer liveth," and subsequently, the "Dead March in Saul." The funeral service was read by the Rev. D. Waller, vicar of St. Paul's Church, Leftwich. The late Mni Henry Jukes, be- longed to a family who for many generations have been engaged in the musical profeettiom The deceased was the 'author of many pieces of music, He took up his abode at Northwich when he was very young and followed the inneical profession in order to gain a livelihood. He had not been there long when lie was appointed organist at Witton Church. This appointment he held for seven years, and he filled a similar position at Castle Church for a like period. He had also been organist at the Roman Catholic Chanel, Birkenhead, and subsequently held the position of organist at the Seale-street Roman Catholic Chapel, Liverpool. He married in 1854 Mrs. Burgoyne, the daughter of Mr. J. Waldrom. Mr. Waldrom was profeisor of music and a dependant of the late Duke of Rutland, from whom he re- ceived a handsome salary. The deceased had four children —twe sons and two daughters.

RUNCORN BauNswrcirNovEarENT CLAss.—At the weekly meeting of this class on Wednesday evening, Mr. R. Norman read an essay on "British Commerce." Mr. T. Simister presided. SUNBEAM JUVENILE TEN:pLE, WIDNES.—The mem- bers of this Temple met for the first time in the new room in Mersey-street on Wednesday evening, when 58 were present. Six new members were initiated, and eleven gave in their names for initiation. A RuNcom TRADING VESSEL IN CoLusroN.—The schooner Abstainer arrived at Runcorn on Tuesday very seriously damaged, through being in collision in the river. The vessel, it appears, was lying at anchor waiting for a convenient tide for Runcorn, when the schoone; Thomas , Ayling came into collision with her, and breaking from her mooring she fell across the bows of the training ship Inde- fatigable. Her main mast was broken, and bowsprits and bulwarks carried away. The vessel is now in Runcorn,where she will be repaired. STAR LODGE I. 0. G. T., WrnNEs. The above lodge held its usual meeting on Wednesday evening, at the lodge-room, Mersey-road. The following officers were in- stalled by Bro. W, B. Clarke, viz. :—Chief templar, Bro. Res- call ; vice-templar, Bro. Johnson; chaplain, Bro. Carter; marshal, Bro. Jones; secretaries, Bros. Bold and Hutton ; financial secretary and treasurer, Bros. Newton and Coleburn ; past chief templar, Bro. Turton. There was a good atten- dance of members, and several names were given in for

FORTHCOMING DRAMATIC PERFORMANCE AT WIDNES.— On Thursday next a dramatic performance, in connection with the Railway Benevolent Institution, will be given at the Drill Hall, Widnes. The programme is one that promises a varied and intellectual entertainment. It will include "As you like it," "The school for scandal," and "The bells." Mr. W. S. Bransom, well known for his felicitous rendering of Shakesperian pieces, will lead the performance; and he will be assisted by Miss Alice Finch, of Biriningham. Among the Weal ladies and gentlemen who have promised their co-operation and assistance are Messrs. Joseph Morrison, McLennan, R. Lewis, H. B. Shores, W. E. Oakden, J. W. White, J. S. Rigby, and Miss Oakdkn. It is stated that arrangements have been made for the productions to be mounted with magnificent scenery. The hall will be decor- ated, and an effort made to improve its acoustic properties. We think the event will thoroughly justify our predictions that the performance will be thoroughly well managed, and that the visitors will spend a very pleasant evening.

MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN : TEA AND ENTER- TAINMENT AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday evening a public tea meeting was held in the mission-room, Bottom Locks, Runcorn, in connection with Runcorn branch of the above missions. The proceeds of the evening are intended to raise funds for carrying on the sewing meetings for a bazaar and sale of work, which it was intended to hold in December, but which has been postponed. The tea was given by Mrs. Whitby and the two Misses Whitby, of Ellesmere Port, and was presided over by several ladies in- terested in the work. About 60 persons eat down to tea, after which an interval of half an hour occurred for the re- moval of the tables previous .to holding a miscellaneous entertainment. In the unavoidable absent of Mr. Thomas Norman, Mr. Rosenberg, of Weston Point, kindly consented to take the chair. In opening the meeting the Chairman, in the course of few general remarks, said he was in a rather difficult position, having to occupy the chair, and at the same time take his part in the programme. It was a rather uncommon thing for a chairman to have to call upon him- self for a song or a reading, but that would be his duty on the present occasion. He was sorry there was not a larger number present, as he felt sure the work that the meeting was intended to help was well worthy of all the assistance they could possibly give; and Mr. Straw, \Ow had the matter in hand, deserved not only their sympathy, hut their support. He ardently hoped that all present would look at it in this light, and be determined to do their very best for so good a work. (Applause.) The entertainment was given by a party of ladies and gentienen from Weston Point, who performed the various parts assigned to them in a manner equally creditable to themselves and pleasing to the audience. Miss Mande Clark acted as accompanist. The programme was as follows :—Glee, "From Oberon in Fairyland," glee party; song, "Jack's come home to-day," Mr. J. Rosen- berg; overture (piccolo and pianoforte), "The Caliph of Bagdad," Miss M. Clark and Mr. Yarwood ; duet, "Ocean shells," Miss M. Clark and Mr. J. Newell ; glee, "The laughing chorus," glee party; pianoforte solo, "The I maiden's prayer," Miss Rosenberg; song," The thorn," Mr. I J. Newall; song, " Maggie's secret," Miss M. Clark; song, " Baby mime," Miss Beale Clark ; reading, "Billy's rose," Mr. J. Rosenberg; glee," Awake, /Ronan Lyre," glee...party ; 1 pianoforte solo," Orazione," Master Grounds; duet," Flow on, thou shining river," Miss Grounds and Mr. Rosenberg; I glee, "Ye Mariners of England," glee party: "God save the Queen." After the usual vote of thanks 110 been given, the proceedings terminated.

, THE RUNCORN MAMMA CLUB'S CONCERT.—ThO , members of this society gave their first concert for the season on Monday in the Public Hall, the work chosen for perform- ance teing Haydn's "Creation." l'he oratorio is so well known, and so deservedly popular, that a description of it is unnecessary. The principals were Madame Bellini Porter, of the Hallo concerts, Mr. J. I. Hodson,tenor,and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint, bass. On this occasion Madame Porter made her debut before a Runcorn audience, and sang the numbers allotted to her in a manner which at once obtained the sympathetic ear of the audience. Her voice is of consider- able compass and power, and of a fairly even quality, and she may be pronounced a pleasing singer. Her rendering of the charming air, "With verdure clad," was thoroughly artistic. She was equally successful in sustaining her part in the trio Most beautiful appear," and evinced meat power of vocalisation and compass of voice in the concluding duet with Adam "Graceful Consort." Mr, Hodson, also new to a Runcorn public, sung the numbers for which he was responsible with taste and expression, and a fidelity to the composer which is often wanting in singers of wider fame. His singing of the air, "The native worth," was really fine, and was listened to with marked attention and delight, and received well merited applause. Mr. Bantock Pierpoint was in excellent voice, and was especi- ally successful in the descriptive aria "Rolling in foaming billow," the recitative "Straight opening," and its sequel "Now heaven in fullest glory shone." He sang all the parts allotted to him in splendid style, and frequently received the well merited plaudits of the discriminating audience. Since their last session the Madrigal Club have organised an orchestral band, consisting of several local gentlemen, and a " fair " violinist of high social position and popularity. This being their first public appearance, they were strengthened by a few members of a Liverpool orchestral society, and performed their onerous duties very creditably, proving a great addition to the personnel and effectiveness of the society. The chorus sustained their Part fairly well, but a want of sufficient previous practice was apparent in the "thinness" which marked the entry of the " leads" in several of the choruses, and the faulty articulation of the words. They gave, however, the chorus, "The heavens are telling," with grand effect, and also the last chorus, "Sing the Lord ye voices all." The conductor (Mr. W. I. Argent, of Birkenhead,) deserves hearty recognition for ..the manner in which he performed his by no means light or unimportant duties, he undertak- ing, in addition, the accompanying on the organ. He is also to be commended for the high standard of music he presents for public criticism and approval, and the marked interest he takes in the musical culture of his classes in Runcorn, Widnes, and Frodsham. We have been given to understand that the Musical Society of Frodsham intend very shortly holding their first coacart under his direction, and that the Runcorn Madrigal Club will also perform the " Messiah " about Christmas. We should hot omit to state that the concert was listened to by a numerous audience, including the elete of the town and district, who by their applause frequently evinced approval and appreciation of the efforts of both principals and chorus. - - COCICHEDGE INFANT SCROOL.—SOMMa Ty of H.M. Inspector's report after the annual examination, November
11th, 1881 :—"This is one of the very best infant schools in my district. The discipline is excellent, and the in.

struction is thoroughly sound anti intelligent. The readiag is fluent and expressive in an uncommon degree. The girls sew very nicely." BRICK .STREET AND FRIARS'-GREEN BAND OF HOPE SOCIETY.—The fourth entertainment of the season in con- nection with the above was held in Friars'e-green school- room, on Tuesday. The chair was taken by Mr. JAS. Shaw, who made a very appropriate address before proceeding with the programme for the evening, in which he dwelt on the different phases of the temperance question, showing that in some of the organisations all shades of temperance , opinions could join hands and yet be consistent, quoting as examples the Alliance and Sunday closing movements. For himself he preferred total abstinence, not only believing in the theory, but in the practice of the same, being a life tee- totaller. He urged the necessity of every Sunday school having its Band of Hope to keep the scholars from the bane- ful influences of the drink. A capital programme, consist- ing of songs, hart-song, recitations, and dialogues, was rendered in a manner which did credit to all concerned, well meriting the signs of approval which marked its course throughout.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT WINWICS —AR inquest was held on Saturday, by Mr. Driffield, touching the death of a man named Patrick Mullen (52), who was employed by Mr. Powlson, of Winwick. On Saturday, the sth inst., deceased went to work, and was then in his usual health. He returned home about half-past seven on Saturday night and said he had been hurt by a falling tree. He was digging the tree up by the roots in the orchard, and when he saw it falling in the opposite direction to that which he wished, he put out his arms to stop it, and thus sustained his injuries. On the Sunday following he kept his bed. Dr. Richmond was called to see deceased, who went several times to the Infirmary. , Deceased complained of a pain in his right side and of his breathing generally. Dr. Richmond, house surgeon at the Infirmary, said he believed pl eur isv to have been the cause of death, arising from the accident. A verdict of "Death from some chest affection, oaused by the injury received frorn the falling tree," was recorded,

RENT REMISSION IN CHESHIRE.—Last evening, at the rent audit of Mr. Naylor, at Hooton, Cheshire, the tenantry on the Hooton Estates again received a remission of 10 per cent on the half-year. THE CHESHIRE STABBING CASE—Henry White, who was stabbed in the back with a knife by another boy a fortnight since, at Ellesmere Port, is now so far recovered that it is expected he will be able to appear to prosecute to-day. SUDDEN DEATH AT WARRINGTON.—The police report the sudden death of Richard Edmund, infant son of Joseph Walmsley, forge labourer, of 4, Hope-street. The child was taken to bed in its usual health at 11-30 on Wednesday night. Two hours later the mother wakened and found the child very ill. In a:quarter of an hour it was dead.

TEE " EXAMINER " AT LATCHFORD.—Having had c.nn plaints from this district of a difficulty in obtaining The Examiner, we wish to inform our readers that it may always be obtained at Mr. Joseph Leigh's, provision dealer, Weir View, Kntstsford-road, Latchford. RENT DINNER AT BEWSET HALL. The tenants of he Hon. Leopold W. H. Powys, numbering 31, at down to an excellent dinner at Bewsey Jan, on Wednesday. The Hon. Leopold Powys was present with a number of friends, and his health was drunk nith much enthusiasm.

GUT TO TELE TOWN OF PRESTON. —At the Preston Town Council, on Thursday, it was announced that Mr. Hodgkinson, president of the Reform Club, had made a gift to the town of a splendid collection of British birds, comprising upwards of 400 specimens and 200 species. A vote of thanks was passed to the donor. FIRE AT WenniNGToN.—The dwelling-house, occu- pied by Mr. James Bellwood, in Old-road, Latchford, was considerably damaged by fire on Monday morning. The fire broke out in the kitchen, hut how it originated is not known. On the fire bell ringing, Inspector Profit with P.O Bruen and fireman Monks at once conveyed a reel cart to the place, but extinguished the fire by buckets of water. Damage to the amount of £lOO was done. The property however, insured in the Lion Insurance Company. TEE LATE Rev. F. S. Hacrxx. The Rev. Thomas Rippon, in concluding his sermon at Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday morning last, made a touching reference to the death of the Rev. F. S. Hagen, which was announced in our last issue. Allusion was also made to the death of the rev, gentleman, at the Wesleyan Chapel, Lymm, and at the conclusion of each service Mr E Brown, organist, played the" Dead march in Saul."

I.O.G.T.—TEMPErtANCE MISSION LODGE—The weekly session of the above lodge was held in the Temperance Mission Room, Academy-street, on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of W.C.T. Bro. G. McNaboe. Mr. Thomas Hall attended and gave an interesting address on " Rechahitism," fully explaining the principles and objects of the Order, and at the conclusion of the address a number of questions put by members of the lodge were satisfactorily answered by Mr. Hall. A hearty vote of thanks was ac- corded to Mr. Hall for his address, and the proceedings terminated.

ST. PAUL'S TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, WARRINGTON. —St. Paul's branch of the Church of England Temperance Society held a meeting in Heath Side Infant School on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. W. Beamont: There was a good audience, and addresses were delivered by the Chairman, Mr. L. P. Stubbs (Liverpool), Mr. Adams, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, and Mr. G. Wood. The proceedings were diversified by recitations and songs. COCKIIEDOE MISSION MCTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY —The fourth meeting of the session was held on Monday, when an essay was real by Mr. James Bridge, entitled, "The deceits of Jacob and its lessons." The essayist showed God's retribution and justice upon Jacob in driving him from his peaceful home, his being deceived by his uncle Ltbon, and at last by being deceived by his own sons with his son Joseph's coat, elm. An animated discussion ensued by the members, the essay being approved of by 29 to 3.

SUDDEN DEATH OF A CIULD AT WARRINOTON.—Mr. C. E. Driffield, connty coroner, held an inquest at Warring- ton, on Saturday, touching the death of a child named Wm. Nnrman, son of William Norman, 49, Wellington-street. The deceased, who was two years and nine months old, on Thursday, the 17th inst., seemed to be ill, and was put on a sofa, where he remained all day. At night he became very quiet, but did not complain of any pain, and his mother gave him a little castor oil. She gat up with him, and about three o'clock gave him a tablespoonful of milk. She then left him, and on returninz about a quarter of an hour afterwards found him dead. She did not call a doctor, but Iwould have done so at once had se thought the child was seriously ill. During his illness deceased was very thilsty , and hot. He had efery attention. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural cams." PROFESSOR Fowntrt AT WArturxriTog. —The course of lectures on "Mental science," which professor Fowler, I the renowned phrenologist, commenced in the Public Hall,. on Monday, and continued until Thursday, attracted larn•e audiences each evening. The subjects comprised advice on "How to read character," hints on "Self culture," the " Revelations of the face," and the "Geniis of love," and were dealt with in an able and interesting manner by the lecturer, who was listened to with the greatest attention throughout. At the con- clusion ef the lectures, Profestor Fowler phrenologicallv examined a number of gentlemen who ascended the platforr;l at his invitation, and in a few minutes he described their characters as faithfully as though he had known them all their lives, the truthfulness of his remarks being admitted by the various gentlemen, and confirmed by thoe of the audience with whom they were acquainted.

SHOCKING END OF A WARRINGTON WHITESMITH.— William Abrahams, a whitesmith, 42 years of age, and residing at 25, Orford-street, Warrington, poisoned himself on Wednesdly under most extraordinary circumstanns. For the last five weeks he had been drinking hard, and during that time he had done no work. He threatened in the presence of his wife aweek ago to commit suicide, and be- haved in a queer manner. On Wednesday morning, Abrahams went home " dead drunk" and turned his wife into the street. She did not return home until half-past three, when she found her husband lying on the bed apparently asleep. She shook him, and then discovered in his left band a small empty bottle labelled " Laudanum, poison." Dr. Joseph, who was immediately called in, said it was a hopeless case, and in half an hour the wretched man expirel. The de- ceased is stated to have obtained two ounces of laudanum from a chemist. The inquest will be held to-day (Sat- urday).

Tint FATAL POACHING AFFRAY IN CHESHIRE—The three men, Perrin, Hitcheas, and Willis were trough t up on remand at the Altrincham Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. W. Jeynson and other magistrates, charged with night poaching on the oth inst., at High Leen on the land of Colonel Legit, and with shooting with intent to murder Thomas Ford, a watcher. Mr. Hockin, who appeared to pro- secute, stated that the prisoners had been remanded in order that an important witness (Ford,) who was under treatment in the Manchester Infirmary, should be there to give evidence Ford, although progressing favourably, was not in such a condition that the gentleman in whose charge be was would allow him to be there that day. He would call Dr. Howlett, and then ask for a further remand. Dr. How- lett said the man was progressing favourably, but the wounds were not sufficiently healed to admit of his coming out yet. The Chairman asked whether it would be dangerous to move him. Dr. Howlett thought so. In reply to the Clerk, he said he thought he would be able to appear that day week. He could articulate but not distinctly. The prisoners were again remanded.

HAMMON'S CIRCUS, WARRINGTON. The entertain- ments provided by Mr. Harmaton still sustain their popu- larity, and this week large audiences have been attracted to the circus by the performances of the " educated " bull Peter. It is a fine young animal, and was purchased by Mr. Harmston from Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P., of Massey Thelwall. It showed a docility and intelligence most unusual in a bull, and went through a surprising perfor- mance. When bade by his keeper, the animal walked round the ring on its knees, lay on the ground, and allowed hitn to stand upon its neck. Then after several evolutions in the rir g, it mounted two pedestals, and revoked on the top, whilst 1 there tiring a gun by pulling the trigger with its mouth, and placed its foot upon the head of the trainer. Its feat of leaping through a five-barred gate, and through a hoop of fire at the same time, was accomplished with ease, and was loudly applauded by the audience. Nothing could be more grotesque than its concluding feat, when dressed in a cape and tall white hat, it mounted the " ThelwwaelrleaCiso,eoaecivilniell'i sustained seized the reins in its mouth, and drove a couple of ponies several times round the ring, and into the stable. Eleven weeks only has been the time occupied in training" Peter" tricks,wltipchroagrreamwmelel worth T do these heother Poartsito°nnsis g interesting of

SATURDAY EVENING CONCERTS AT Sr. HELENS. —MT. Barton's third concert of this class this season was held on Saturday. The Walton Breck Glee Union made their firs appearance in the Town Hall, but there were too many defects in their singing to evoke much sympathy from the audience. There was a lack of spirit in the singing, of "Comrades to arms." This was rendered more conspicuous, perhaps, by the way in which the song was " dragged " along. Miss Annie Richardson sang a couple of contralto songs in a beautiful style, and Madame Paltnira Bonvini contributed some pleasing pieces. Mr. W. A. McClures's singing met with the highest marks of approval from the company who seemed especially delighted with " A father's love" and "The village blacksmith." Some "Tyrolean and Anglo-Dutch " characters were portrayed by Mr. T. W. Hall, and Mr. A. C. Carr sung by desire "A warrior bold." Mr. Barton, who is always welcome in musical circles, sang "Farewell my mountain life." Miss Emily Gardner, with , her accustomed ability, presided at the piano. To-night (Saturday) Mr. Lester Barrett will give character sketches.
TROOPS IN WAngnuoTorr.—Seventy-five members of the 2nd Dragoon Guards, queen's Bays, en route from Limerick to Manchester, were billetted in town on Monday night.

PEPECOT POLICE Cotatz—On Tuesday, before Mr. W. L. Evans, James Collins and Thomas Burns were charged with deserting from the 40th Brigade DepOt, at Warrington. On Sunday evening P.C. Howarth met the prisoners on Warrington-road, Rainhill, and as they could not produce passes he took them into custody. Prisoners were remanded to Walton gaol to await an escort.—On Wed- ' nesday, John McCowlef, a carter in the employ of Mr. 'Harrison, of St. Helens, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart, at Derby-street, , Prescot, on the previous day. DRAM 07 Ma. JOHN HARRISON, 07 ST. Haman. It is with regret that we announce the death, which took place suddenly on Monday morning between two and three o'clock, of Mr. John Harrison, plasterer, Westfield-street. Mr. Harrison WAS 55 years of age, 27 of which he spent in St. Helens. He was held in great respect by those with whom he did business, and the members of the St. Helens Permanent Benefit Building Society, with which society he had been connected 24 years. He was also a member Of the Masonic body. Mr. Harrison leaves behind him a widoi, and a family of six daughters and three sons. He was attended by Drs. Gaskell and Hay, and Dr. Bickerstaffe, of Liverpool. • MAT /lowa JUVENILE TEMPLE 1.0.G.T. No. 1,253, ST. HELENS.—An entertainment of an interesting character was given on Tuesday, in the United Methodist Free Church school. Mr. T. Thompson, who presided, urged all present to shun the intoxicating cup, and train the young in habits of sobriety. A song by Mrs. Lindon, super- intendent of the temple, "Prevention is better than cure," was given in her usual good style, and heartily applauded. Mr. Kiddie gave "Found dead," which was well encored, after which he gave a piece entitled "Confession." Miss Wells gave one of her Lancashire recitations. "How to cure a brutal husband," with her usual ability, and was loudly applauded. Mr. James Servant gave an interesting address, and encouraged all to do what they could to impede the drink traffic. Mr. T. Pickersgill spoke chiefly to the chil- dren, taking for his motto, "Nursery rhymes; "and songs and recitations were given by Misses Susan Kiddie, Lilly Gore, Martha Whitehead, Mary Kiddie, Eccleston, Earth Gore Messrs. Edward Friar, %William 'Kiddie, and Miss Sarah Davies. The attendance was goo I.

div.head: UNITED KINGDOM ALUINCE.
div.p: UNITED KINGDOM ALUINCE.
MEETING AT RUNCORN.

A meeting which bad only been indifferently advertis,cl was held in the Bethesda Congregational Schcolroont, at Runcorn, on the evening of the 18th met., in connection with the United Kingdom Alliance. There was a poor attendance. The Rev. J. D. Thomas presided. Speeches from Mr. D Bisbrown and Mr. J. D. Jones were made in moving the following resolution:—" That this meeting most earnestly calls upon the social reformers, friends of tem- perance, education, religion, and public order in the various constituencies throughout the United Kingdom, to render all possible aid to the Alliance and the various temperance organisations co-operating with it, so as more fully to arouse the conscience of the nation and influence the electors to make a determined stand against its greatest social pest end curse, and to give such united electoral support to the men and measures as will suppress the facilities and temptations to intemperance, and confer upon the people the power to veto the issue of licenses for the sale of intoxicating liquors within their respective psrishes and districts."—Mr. C. H. MURRAY, deputation from the Alliance, supported the motion, and in his opening remarks alluded to the speech on the connection between drink and crime of Justice Kay at the Liverpool Assizes. It had been said that teetotallers used very strong language, and slandered their friends the publicans. He had no wish to slander anybody, for he was of opinion that the moment they stepped beyond the truth they did harm to their cause. Not many years ago an article Was written, and thought to be so good that it was printed in a prominent magazine. It transpired that this article was written by a brewer, and was entitled "The evils of intem- perance and how to stop them." The article was most ably written, and touched all sides so powerfully that the tee- totallers were delighted, and it was reprinted by them, al- though strongly objected to by the writer. After speaking on the crime and pauperism brought on by drink, the article says:—"lt is not too much to say that there are no less than half a million houses in the United Kingdom where home happiness is never known from this one cause." It then went on to speak of the bad effect this must have upon the children growing up in those homes. If what the writer stated was true, was jr not IMUMbent upon them to look intO krtiait a social disarrangernedt? Temperatiet advocates had not gone farther than they could prove to be correct; and they called upon all possessing any influence at all to aid them in their endeavours to sweep away the great evil. It was a matter especially belonging to the people, and they wanted the people to deal with it. It was only fair "that the man who paid the piper should have the right to choose the tune," and if the people of this country had to meet all the burdens which drink brought upon them, it WAG , only Het that ley should be able to say whether they I would submit to the evil or not. (Applause.) It was said that the trade was for their convenience, but if they did not see the convenience and resented the nnitaance, then they bad a right to exercise a power. To a certain extent they had local option, and wished to alter the law very little. At present the magistrates had the power of granting licenses, and what the Alliance meant by local option was to set aside the power of the magistrates and have the matter in their own hands. (Applause.) Some people were very anxious about the revenue when temperance people spoke of the great evil, and he was astonished to see the anxiety they mani- fested lest the Chancellor of the Exchequer should not have money enough to meet his liabilities. For his own part he was quite willing to let the Chancellor mind his own busi- ness. (Laughter and applause.) But was it not a disgrace that the income of the country should be kept up by money derived from that which was admitted by all to be a social curse. No country ever fell from greatness to dishonour and degradation through a greater nation overpowering them. All nations that had so fallen had done so from the direful influence of vice which had sapped the vitality and power of the people. (Applause.) If they degraded their people then their greatness could not last long—(applause)—and they were on a sure way to decal and ruin. Out of the £122,000,000 spent in drink the Government received £30,000,000, and if those people who troubled themselves so much about the finallCeS of the country would give the Government threepence out of the shilling they now spent in drink and saved the other ninepence the revenue would not be harmed. Let them remember that the moment they removed the drink they removed their burdens. There were the burdens of their prisons, and pauperism, and three-fourths of the latter were traceable to drink. Many political econo- mists believed that if the people paid taxes directly instead of indirectly, and knew what they were paying, that Eng- land could ba governed for less than £80,000,000 a year. (Applause.) It was high time they wiped from the nation's fair fame the dark blot of having to keep up the country from a revenue obtained from a curse; and he asked them to help in removing so great an evil from their midst. (Ap- plause. )—Th e motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. ‘VILLIAM HANDLEY moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Murray for his interesting address. He thought they were greatly indebted to the United Kingdom Alliance for the way in which they promulgated their views, and the efforts they had made to promote sobriety and to place in the bands of the people a constitutional right. It was time that the con- science of the nation was aroused on the great question of the day. As a Guardian he knew that three-fourths of the paupers that he bad to do with had been brought to that low position through intemperance, and he was glad to see that the churches had been aroused to the evils around them. He regretted that there were not more present that night, but he remembered that, years ago, in order to make a meeting of that kind a successful one, they held a conference previous to it, and brought clearly before the people the objects of the Alliance. He was glad to hear that was only to be the first of a series of meetings, and be thought if a conference was held previous to the meetings they would be more sntcessful. (Applause.)—Mr. W. SHAW seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously—Mr. MURRAY, in responding, approved of a conference, and said the Alliance were pre- pared to do all they could to arouse the public to action in he movement.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

ALLEGED THEFT AT GOLBORNE.—Peter McLoughlin, drawer, Golborne, was brought before Mr. Artingstall, at Mr. Buckton's office, Werington, on Monday, charged with stealing half a crown from the Church Inn on the previous Friday evening, the property of Ann Pilling.—Mr. Moore appeared for tbe defence.—Prosecutrix stated that on the evening in question she sold a box for half a crown. She placed the money on the table, and asked the landlady to Change it, whereupon prisoner offered to change it, hut in- stead of doing so he picked up the coin and walked off.— Prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, was remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions, bail being allowed. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, LOWTON-ROAD, GOL- BORNE.—Mr. James Tipton's " Eva," a musically illustra- ted service of song, compiled and arranged from the well- known story or "Uncle Tom's Cabin," was given in the above place of worship on Saturday evening, by the chapel choir, to a moderate attendance. Mr. Twist presided, and Mr. David Lord read the the connective readings, which de- pict the horrors of the slave 'rade. The leading features of the piece were rendered additionally strikiug by the simple but adequate melodies running through the entire service, the most effective of which was perhaps Harwood' s " Vital spark." Mr. Taylor accompanied the choir, which was under the leadership of Mr. W. Entwistle. The proceeds of the service will be devoted to the harmonium fund. GOLDORNE WESLEYAN CHAPEL—At a church meeting, held on Monday, the contemplated scheme adopted by the members some time ago of pewing the chapel and building a school was further considered, and a number of subscrip- tions promised in aid of the undertaking. At present the building is utilised both for school and chapel purposes, and the advisableness of providing separate school accommoda- tion and making the chapel more comfortable and attractive is constantly forcing itself upon the members, who have decided to proceed with the work as soon as sufficient funds are obtained to sanction such a step. A number of collectors have been appointed to solicit donations from friends. Messrs. Eutwistle and Seddon are the secretary and treasurer respectively.
LATEST NEWS.
_ Mr. Bright has consented to fax the foundation _of 11011 new Board Schools at Llandudno on December Bth. A .7A4 Bright scholarship will be founded in commemoration it the event. • •

At Boyle fair, yesterday, a farmer named May was as tacked by a young man named Pointer, with whom he had a dispute respecting some Lind, and was so severely beatstt with a loaded whip that his life is despaired of. Pointer has been arrested.

For the past week an organizer from 11,e Dublin Ladies Land League has been travelling County Waterford witk the object of establishing branches in the different towns, but up to last night he had but formed one branch through- out the whole county. Last ni4ht twelve sheep the property of Lord Doneraile, near Cork, were killed and thirty others so seriously mimed th it they will have to be killed. His lordship recently served writs for non-payment of rent ost several tenants.

Two snits of apartments in Hampton Court Palace vacant by the death of the Hon. Mrs. Cuthbert, and Mrs. Doherty have been bestowed upon Licty Colley, widow of Sir G. Pomeroy Colley, and Mrs. Lambert, widow of Admiral Rowley Lambert.

The trial of Guiteau for the murder of President Garfield is proceeding. Witnesses for the defence state that he showed symptoms of "moral imbecility," but their evident* so far is hardly worth a moment's consideration. The assassin continually interrupts the witnesses, and offers com- ments and suggestions which sometimes provoke laughter, but generally excite disgust. BARRACKS FOR THE SALVATION A mfr.—General Booth has resolved upon purchasing a large property, built for the London Orphan Asylum, at Clapton, London, at a cost £23,000, and adapting it for "a great national barracks UK the training of officers, and a large congress ball." The latter is to accommodate nearly 5.000 persons, and there are to be class and drill rooms for 3,000 persons. The property originally cost over £60,000. On Thursday morning a small revolver was found near te the rails on the London and Brighton lin, about 25 miles from London. It was empty and had been considerably damaged. The weapon was shown to the pawnbrokers with whom Lefroy pledged, and from whom he redeemed, the pistol so often referred to in the course of the trial, and they are decidedly of opinion that it is the same.

Four dead bodies have been washed ashore on Keadue strand, county Donegal, and have been identified as those of pers ms belonging to the Island of Innishkeeragh. Cat. munication from the mainland has been impossible for some time past, but it is feared that the island, which is a very low lying one, has ben swept by the Atlantic daring the terrible storm on Monday last, when immense damage was done along the west coast of Ireland. A FISH DEALER SENT TO ratsoll.—At the Liverpool Police Court, yesterday, Mary Maher, a fish dealer, was charged by warrant with exposing for sale 337 herrings which were unfit for human food. Inspector G. J. Robinson said that on the 19th inst. he examined a box containing 337 herrings, wh ch were exposed for sale in the avenue near the fish market, Great Charlotte-street, and found the fish to be rotten and unfit for food. The prisoner, who had been twice fined and once committed for similar offences, was sent to gaol for 20 days without the option of a fine.

THE GREAT DIAMOND ROBBERY. Although we are unable to give particulars of exact contents of the packages stolen from Hatton Garden post office, we are officially in- formed that of the 36 registered packets 14 contained rough and cut diamonds, sapphires. etc.' to the.value of £14,330. The other valuables comprised watches, chains, rings, bracelets, and postage stamps, the gross amount for which they were insured being £14,821. Oae package of diamonds was insured for £5,000, another for £4,000, a third for £2,500, and the others for much smaller amounts. Yesterday afternoon Mr. Young, solicitor, applied at the Thames Police Court, on behalf of the Society for Preven- tion of Cruelty to Animals, for a summons against a Colonial broker named Lanacbe, who carried on business in the city, for cruelty. Mr. Young explained that the gentleman complained of had a consignment of live tor. tomes from abroad, the creatures being tightly packed in barrels, and after being landed were allowed to remain for ten days unpacked. A discussion took place as to whether tortoises were domestic animals, but the summons was finally granted.

TILE FLOGGING or GIRLS.—The directors of the Glasgow Industrial School are continuing their private hivestigatioa into the alleged cruelty in the school, pending the arrival of a Government inspector. It is stated that the officials speak of the punishments as being tPrrityle and freauent. A little girl who had 1 stolen a lola bad to carry it in a bag on her back for a we, alter which she had to eat a slice every day till it was finished. Flogging was not the only punish- ment, because on repeated occasions children for some offence were forced to swallow large quantities of salt. Another little offender, who was accused of stealing a half-crown, received twenty-one stripes in nearly a nude state. On asserting her innocence she, it is said, received seventeen I other strokes.

div.head: LEFROY'S CASE.
div.p: LEFROY'S CASE.

We understand the Home Secretary has decided against any medical examination of Lefroy on behalf of the con- vict's relatives. Should Sir William Harcourt himself have any doubts on this subject he would refer to the prison surgeon's official report. Itwill be remembered that the Home Secretary was asked to allow doctors Forbes, Wins- low, and Winn to visit Lefroy, but, as from their published letters these gentlemen may be regarded as already enter- taining strong doubts as to the prisoner's sanity, one of the relatives has suggested that an independent medical gentle- man might be sent down to Lewes, and the name of Dr. Graham Bennett., of Hertford-street, Mayfair, has been mentioned in this connection, but it is not considered likely the Home Secretary will alter his decisioa on Vile matter. Dr. Winn, one of the gentlemen before before referred to, has written last night another letter, in which he says the United States has given Guiteau the benefit of the opinions of experts, and asks why Leroy should not have the same privilege.. He mentions the hereditary prOisposition to insanity in the prisoner's family, the convict's marked delusions, his uration a conduct, and his epileptic attacks cn Epsom racecourse, as reasons why a competent medical examination should be made. THE RIGHT HON. JOHN BRIGHT ON PROTECTION. The following letter has been addressed to a gentleman at Newport (Isle of Wight), by Mr. Jonn Bright in reply to questions on the subject of protective duties. "One Ash, Rochdale.—Dear Sir,—lf you keep a particular trade em- ployed at the cost of taxing persons engaged in other trades, what is it but a system of relief or like feeding a dog with its own tail? Our people are not turned out of work by foreign imports. How do we employ and feed ten millions of increased population since the Free Trade era, or since 1840? They are far better employed and paid and fed now than they were forty years age, when they were ten millions Ices in number. The present state of things is one of steady and general improvement, and poor rates are decreasing everywhere. All these ideas are delusions and falsehoods. Yours truly, " Nov. 20th. "Jone Bnicarr." [Read Mr. Redley's Reciprocity Craze, published by Messrs. Cassell, retter and Galpin, for facts.]
