div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 26, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 26, 1881.

TRAVELS IN THE EAST. BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [Spncter..3 XXVI. SAFED. The city stands on the face of a steep hill, with the houses rising one above another, as if the back wall of the lower houses teemed the foundation of the front wall of those behind. We passed up a lane in the outskirts of the town to the rigkt, and found our tents had been pitched clots by, nay, in the very midst of a Moslem burying place, and I within a short distance of a circular meend, on which are the uins of a tower or castle, supposed to have been built by the Frenck in the time of the Crusaders. Perched up here, 3,400 feet above the level of the sea, the city has been twice destroyed by earthquakes; once in 1795 and again in ILS37. Oa .the last occasion no fewer than 5,00 C persons out of a population of 9,000 perished by the falling of the houses one upon another, when the earth yawned in great chasms, and brought them toppling down. Br. Thompson, the American missionary, was an eye-witness, and mentions that, in addition to the thousands crushed and mangled. great numbers were buried alive and died of hunger. The Turkish Government afforded no assistance, to the Protes- tants in their almost super-human efforts to extricate the sufferers. Tiberias also Buffered very greatly from the same earthquake ; and it was noticed that, previous to the shock, the hot spring was much hotter and. more copious in its flow for some days. The level part of the town of Safed, as it is spread out on the top of this the highest hill in Galilee, is built in better style than most Syrian towns. The market-place is unique, which can scarcely be said, from a Syrian point of view, of the trades and merchandise exposed beneath the arches that run around the square. The mechanical trades are carried on with tools of aetede- luvian origin; and I think oranges were about the most rare things offered for sale. Of the mechanics I will give a specimen. One of the p ilanquins by which our cavalcade ' was attended needed some alteration, and a joiner was sent for. In order to make a hole in the wood he used a drill, as is used in England for boring iron. Thie was fixed at the end of a wooden handle. Around the handle he wrapped a piece of leathern-cord fastened from end to end of a rod, which he worked to and fro like a fiddle-stick. Of course, before he got well into the wood the tool became as hot as fire, and it took him several minutes to make a hole which an English workman would have made in five seconds. So the poor fellow tolled and perspired, as his forefathers in the trade had done for a hundred generations before him, all for want of a little skill to produce the gimblet or the more perfect brace-and-bit. We thought when we left the Sea of Galilee in the morning that we had lost sight of it for ever. Judge, then, of the pleasure and surprise we experienced when, in going to the brow of the hill, looking south, we saw it lying, apparently at a short distance, placidly embosomed between the bills of Galilee and Ganialia. Although we were 2,700 feet above its level, and 15 to 20 miles away, it seemed as if we could have run down to its shores in a few minutes, such was the effect of tire purity of the atmosphere in effacing distance. Had it not been for a light haze that hung over the more distant landscape, we should have seen from this elevation the bed of the Jordan for many miles' and away over the mountains and table-lands of Gilead and Moab—a sight I coveted very much. The night, as it closed in, had a very stormy look, but, like many other threatening storms in the Holy Land, it passed over quite harmlessly. In our tents we passed the quietest night we had done since we landed at Joppa. Every night, up to this time, our Arab watchmen, frequently sit- ting close to our heads, though outside the tent, kept up a continued change of signals, with the object, as I thought, of keeping each other awake, and so securing our safety. First, there was a sharp whistle, and then a sudden call, to which there were responses from a distance all night through. No one seemed to be disturbed by it but myself. My sleep Ives so much broken that 1 asked the dragoman at last whether such a system was really needful for the safety of the camp. He answered by putting a stop to it at once, which secured to us at Sated the first quiet night we had in Palestine. SAFED TO KADESH NAPTHALI. In former excursions it had been usual to tent near to the waters of Merom, but wiser counsels lutd decided that we should proceed by the higher mountain tracks, and so escape the malaria arising from the swampy plains around the lake. From the elevation we thus obtaieed, we had a suc- cession of delightful views opening out between the mountains, with the waters of Merom giving variety and beauty to the landscape. Then we had a stretch of finely cultivated table-land, and afterwards came upon one of the most fearful mountain gorges lever descended. In leading my horse down its narrow ledges of rock and broken paths, I had to keep my eyes steadily fixed on the ground to pre- vent the dizziness which the tremendous height and steep- ness would have produced. At the bottom we had a fertile valley, with a cool and refreshing stream at our feet, and immense rocks towering above our heads. Here, under some noble trees, we spread our noon-day repast, and spent in various ways a couple of hours afterwards. I was greatly interested in a primitive flour-mill, which in some way or other was worked by water-power. When I first looked in I thought it was a very dirty byre or stable. Two or three donkeys were standing fetlock high in mud and manure. These I found afterwards were waiting to convey their [owners, with the corn they had brought to grind, back to their homes. Picking my way past the donkeys I beheld the mill-stone about two feet in diameter slowly revolving. in a rude trough, into which it was depositing the flour ; above the mill-stone, hanging by ropes from the beam, was a wooden funnel dropping almost grain by grain the corn in- to the antie of the *stone. Three or four women were sitting near to the stone awaiting their turn, and evidently prepared to spend a whole day, if necessary, on the business. Doubt- less the water-mill would be regarded as a grand public in- stitution wonderfully adapted for the saving of labour; but, eurely, "two women grinding at a mill" at borne would have done more work in the time, and saved all the trouble and expense of bringing the cona over such tremendous bills as those by which the mill was surrounded. The mountain track by which we left the valley was as steep and difficult as the one by which we descended into it. One hour's ride, however brought us in sight of Kadesli Napthali, and we were truly thankful, as we reached our tents, on a plateau above the town, to know that we had come to the close of another week, and that another day's journey would bring us to the borders of northern Palestine. The desire for news from home beeline, at this point, almost sickening in its intensity. We had been nearly three weeks without letters, and until we got to Damascus on the Wednesday following we had no chance of hearing a word.

EXTRAORDINARY CONDUCT OF A PRESCI a GIRL. Some excitement was created in Prescot, on Saturday evenimg, by the report that a girl named Mary O'Neil (whose parents reside in Prescot), had been violently assaulted and robbed of a purse containing 10s. in gold, whilst on her way to Prescot early on that evening. O'Neil called at the police office on S tturd ly evening about seven o'clock, and stated that she left Littie.,yood Farm at about half-past five o'clock for the purpose of coming to Prescot. Before starting Mrs. Lyon lent her half-a-sovereign to buy he self a pair of boots. She put the purse and half- sovereign in a small basket which she carried in her band. She walked along the road, and when nearly opposite to Lyon's wash-house in Knowsley-lane, a man came up to her apparently out of the field, and inquired the way to Knotty Ash. While answering him a second man came up and asked her if she had any money. She replied that she had not but would have some on her return as she was going to meet her mother. The man then swore at her, and said he would have either her money or her life He struck her a a severe blow on the right side of the head, and opening the basket took the purse and the half sovereign out. She screamed and the men went away. She then came on to Prescot and went to the house of Miss Atherton, in High- field.place to whom she complained of the outrage.- P.C. Cruikshanks waa at once sent to make inquiries into the affair along the route traversed by the girl. He waited upon Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, her employers, and ascer- tained that Mrs. Lyon never gave the girl half-a- sovereign. She gave her Is. 401. to purcbase a few small articles at Prescot and she =only believed that was , the only money the girl had in her possession when she left , the helm. Whilst the constable was in Mr. Lyon's house, ' O'Neil came in, walked through the room where the officer I was sitting, and called Mrs. Lyon to her. She then stated that after leaving the house for Prescot she met a man whom she knew (out declined to say who he was) and asked him to lend her 10s. to boy a pair of boots. He lent her a half a sovereign and she gave him the purse and is. 4d. Miss Atherton to whose house O'Neil went on getting into Prescot,statedthat when she (O'Neil), came to her place she had is. 4d. in her pocket. After staying in her house,a short time she went to a ehop and purchased a pair of stockings for Mrs. Lyon, for which she paid Is. When questioned about the is. 4d. O'Neal said she had borrowed it from her mother, but, as a matter of fact, her mother had never seen her that day previous to her buying the stockings, and denied ever lending her any money. Before O'Neil returned to Knowsley she went again to the police office and made the same report to Mr. Barker, the snperintendent, and requested that a constable might be sent with her to protect her as she was afraid to go alone, but Mr. Barker wisely declined. Mr. Barker informs us that during the short time he has been the superintendent in the Prescot division, simildr eroundless, and untruthful gtatpnents have been made to him on nuns: than one occasion. It l 5 a great pity that those who make them cannot be punished in somA form or other.

NICK•NAMING A SCHOLAR : COMPLAINT AGAINST THE MASTER. The following letter, from Mr. William Bradshaw, dated 26, Cross-street, Prescat, November 7th, 1881, was read "I wish to draw your attention to the following case is your school. There is a boy named Henry Parr, residing with his mother, who is a widow, near me, and I learn it is a common occurrence with the head master, Mr. Lightfoot, to call him 'Young Zulu,' in fact he exclaimed to the other ' boys very frequently, 'Bring the young Zulu here whilst I give him a pill.' The result of this is that the lad has got this nickname fastened on him, and boys in the street are continually shouting after him, and applying this epithet to him. It has naturally created a dislike against the master and the school. If a stop be not put to it, the lad, who is of a stupid turn of mind, will doubtless refuse to go to the school and be a means .of giving his mother considerable trouble. I wish the board to understand that I have no desire to make the boy into a saint, for I know him to be like most boys, full of wickedness. But inasmuch as he is a nephew of mine, and without the protection of a father, I I consider it my duty to interest myself in his behalf. I can , bring plenty ef evidence if necess try to sustain my charge against the master."—Mr. LIGETFOOT said he only called the boy by that name on one occasion, and that was whilst he and the boys were having a bit of fun in the school- yard.—Mr. SANDERS : It is said to be a common occurrence. —Mr. LIGHTFOOT : Oh, no.—Mr. HEWITT said Mr. Light- foot was in a position that ought to be above that sort of thing, even in the school-5 ard.—Mr. BROWN was disposed to think that a name of that kind might be applied very innocently indeed.—Mr- LIGHTFOOT remarked that the boy had never complained to him,—The matter then dropped.

SINGULAR ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS, NARROW ESCAPE. In the beginning of the present week the weather was very boisterous, and we have to record another accident, which happily was not attended by fatal consequences, as was the case some few weeks ago when it was our sad duty to record the painful accident at Sutton National Schools, which was occasioned by the hurricane which swept over this part of the country at the time. An accident occurred, however, on Tuesday morning about ten minutes to three, which cannot be said to be otherwise than remarkable. .Mr. John Mackay, traveller for Mr. Webster, wine and spirit merchant, was in bed with his family at Heath Field House, near the Old Toll Bar, when the accident occurred. Mr. Mackay, his wife, and the baby being in the outer room, nearest the Old Toll Bar, the next front room being occu- pied by two little girls whose ages are five and eight years, and the room behind that of Mr. and Mrs. Mackay, occupied by a boy ten or eleven years of age. The wind was very boisterous, and owing to a slight accident that had hap- pened to Mrs. Mackay's leg the heads of the family were awake. At the time mentioned the chimney, which was three yards high fell Nvith a loud crash on the roof, making a hole therein about seven or eight yards in circumference. The falling of the bricks, slates, lattices, and mortar con- tinued for about a minute to the great consternation of the family. The first thing that Mrs. Mackay did was to cover the baby with the pillow and await results, but she was greatly frightened, despite the efforts of her husband to soothe her. The next thing to do was to examine the several bedrooms to see if the children had suffered by the accident. The hole in the roof extended over portions of two bedrooms; that in which the boy slept being unclisturly_d. The screams of the two little girls, it was found, arose more from the fright they had sustaiued than actual injury, but their escape was almost miraculous. One of the bricks had alighted on the pillow, and grazed the face of one of the children, while another brick had dropped further into the middle of the bed. The bed was also covered with a large quantity of mortar, ,bc. Mr. and Mrs. Mackay's bedroom was the one in which most damage was done. Under the large hele in the roof was a pair of drawers the top of which was completely smashed in, and otherwise disfigured by the marks occasioned by the falling of the heavy material. This piece of furniture was placed against the inner wall. In the centre of the room was the bed which. with the exception of a few marks, sustained no injury. The bed, a week or two ago, was moved to its present place from the position in which the drawers now stand. Some small articles were broken, and a gold brooch with diamond, worth a considerable amount of money, was lost amongst the debris. We may state that three young people, cousins of Mrs. Mackay, in some other part of the country, were killed by the fall of a chimney which fell in a similar manner to the one at Heath Field House. The house belongs to Mr. Roby, brass founder, Rainhill. It is supposed that the chimney had been rendered defective by the recent stormy weather. Standing, as it does at the Prescot end ot a line of semi-detached houses and exposed to the wind from that quarter, the work begun five weeks ago, required only a day or two of gusty weather to complete its destruction. This was accomplished on Tuesday morning, the chimney being blown down, with the exception of about six bricks.

KADESII. At Kadesh Napthali we stood on time-honoured ground, but ground darkened by many idolatries. It was the place from which Barak sprung, and from which he went forth at the call Of Deborah te liberate the Israelites from the thral- dom of Jabin, king of eanaan, the captain of whose host was Sisera. We visited the remarkable ruins in the neigh- bourhood, a few minutes' walk from the encampment. On the way we passed a large covered-in reservoir, in front of which a number of large marble sarcophagi had been con- verted into drir.lring fountains or troughs for Cattle, Some Of thoNo i elks of the ancient city's wealth and grandeur, as kseen in her ability to glorify her dead, still retain the out- lines of beautifully carved rosettes. Further on we came to a very peculiar structure. It had the appearance of being built with large sauare blocks of stone, put together without ' mortar or cement, and, though shaken loose and standing out in various directions, still sticking together anl pre- serving its original shape. It is supposed to have been a tomb. It is 'built in the square cruciform style, with one dome crowning the four recesses and centre—very simple but very impressive as a piece of architecture. Passing on we came to the ruins of an old temple or synagogue, most likely the former, and a memorial of Israel's idolatries. It I must have been built in the same rich and gorgeous style as the synagogue at Capernaum—the Tyro-Grecian—which is seen in its highest perfection at Baalbee In its early history, Kadesh was honoured being appointed a city of refuge, but must soon have corrupted its way, as its inhabi- tants were carried into captivity by Tiglath Pelizer when he tobk the ten tribes into Assyria. (To be continued next week.)

N'Y EBNER/la.—Before Mr. Thompson, judge. AN ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE PAYMENT OF DEBT.—Mr• Cope- land, on behalf of his creditors, sued Samuel Hayes, of Prescot, for a sum of 13s. 3d. Judgment had been obtained on a former occasion, and the defendant now pleaded pay- ment of debt, which had been acknowledged by Copeland. Copeland, on hearing this, exclaimed, in great excitement, that if the debt was his own he would have the defendant prosecuted for perjury. Defendant called James Lawren- son, who said that he remembered the. writ of execution being put into the house of Samuel Hayes on the 18th July last year. He went down with defendant to Cepeland's house, and saw Copeland in the shop. Defendant paid there and then some money (4s) to Copeland, and asked for a receipt, but Copeland said no receipt was required. Cope- land further stated tbat he did not want his wife to know,— Copeland : How did you know that was a writ for execu- tion?—Witness : I was with him when he received it.— Copeland : Are you a relation of his ?_Witness: Yes; I am hie son-in-law.—t Copeland : This man pleaded poverty, and he was told he had better come down to see me, to ask for time to pay. Ile did come down, and I received from I him that day 4s. I asked Mr. Tabernacle, to whom the estate belongs, to pay 4s. into court, but by an oversight on the part of Mr. Tabernacle's clerk this had not been done. It was only six weeks since I asked him to pay the debt, and he never then disputed it. It is a piece of the grossest perjury ever given.—Mr. Stewart, a bailiff, was called by plaintiff, and he stated that defendant said he had paid the money to the plaintiff's agent. He mentioned this to Cope- land, who said lie had received part of the money. Cope- laud also said that he (witness) might let the warrant stand over.—Copeland: Certainly; I did not want to punish the man, I told him I would give him time, and that he could pay 2s. a week, but that I wanted the money badly.—His Honour: Where is the 45. ?_Copland: I asked Mr. Tabe- rnacle to pay it in.—His Honour :Is he here 2—Copeland: I will have him in in two minutes.--Mr. Tabernacle, on arriving, said the non-payment of the 4s. had been an omis- sion, but Mr. Copeland had asked him to pay the money in several times.— Defendant: I have two more witnesses, who will say that Copeland that night told me that I should hear nothing more about it—Copeland : Certainly; nothing more about the execution.—His Henour : How will you pay it ? It is always the way with such people. If you give , way a bit, and receive money in part, they will turn round upon you.—Mr. Tabernacle: I have found it so in several cases, your Honour.—The amount was then reduced to Ps. 3d., and 2s. 6d. a month allowed, with costs. THE " SHAYMNESS " OF AN INSURANCE COMPANY.— Henry Webster, aged 21, 16, Glover-street, sued the London and Manchester Insurance Company far £1 6s. Bd., for Rick pay.—Mr. Riley appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the defendants.—Mr. Riley said His Honour , would have no hesitation, after hearing the evidence, in coming to the conclusion that plaintiff was entitled to the amount sued for. On the let August plaintiff, who was a labourer, became sick and declared himself on the society. He was attended by Dr. Garton during his sickness. He remained ill of typhoid fever for three weeks and four days, and during that time bad complied with the conditions as laid down by the society's rules. While be was at home one of the officers of the company, Mr. Speed, called at his house and asked for Mr. Webster, meaning the father of the plaintiff. He was informed that be was out. On the 26th August defendants wrote to plaintiff to say that their officer 1 had called at his house and had found him out, which was 'against the rules of the society; and that he would there- fore be disentitled to any further sick pay. Mr. Riley said that a clause referred to in the rules would have permitted plaiutiff to go out, although he did not do so. Plaintiff had only received 103. for the first week, and the claim was made for the remaining portion of the time.—Mr. J. 0. Swift con- tended that when the inspector called plaintiff was out, and plaintiff had also neglected to send him certificates. Both these requirements were set down in the rules. He admitted that plaintiff had sent certificates for the first two weeks.— Mr. Riley called a witness viho proved that Webster had offered a certificate, which the agent refused.—His Honour e.,A that the case showed the shabbiness of the Insurance Company by the Manner in which they tried to evade their liabilities. They objected in the first instance to pay, under a misconception, and when they received information which removed the objections they held back upon various trivial objections, none of which could be substantiated. There was is difference between the evidence, but Mrs. Webster was more to be trusted than Mr. Speed; aud he had greet pleasure in giving a verdict for plaintiff, with costs. CLAIM BY a NnwsParert PeorutEron.—Bernard August Dromgoole, for whom Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared, sought to recover £lO 4s. 6d. from Joseph Hill, auctioneer, and officer to the Sheriff of Lancashire.—Mr. J. 0. Swift said the amount was admittedly due to the plaintiff from some one, and the only question that would arise would be whether by any previous judgment Mr. Dromgoole was debarred from proceeding against the defendant Hill. 'Hill and a man Kenyon formerly carried on business, in partnership, but bolero that Hill had become liable to two items amounting to 30s. for advertising. An accoun,' after they had gone into partnership, was run up to £2l 55.81. At the time of the dissolution of partnership plaintiff understood that Kenyon was going to pay all the accounts, and consequently sued him for the amount, and recovered judgment against him, by I consent, for that sum. That judgment had not been satis- -1 fled, only £1 having been paid on account. The question I now was whether be could sue Hill severally for £lO 4s. 61 —Mr. Byrom, of Wigan, who appeared on behalf of the , defendant, said that judgment having been given, the matter rested simply between Hill and Kenyon. He might say that Mr. Hill had actually paid the amount sued for to Mr. Kenyon. —Mr. Swift admitted that all the accounts were placed together when they entered into partnership.—llis , Honour: 'Well, this is treated as a partnership debt.—Mr. I swift; Hewever Mr. Dromgoole treated it, Mr. Hill seems to be severally liable to it. When the dissolution took place Dromgoole was informed that Mr. Kenyon would pay all the accounts; and he thought that Kenyon would pay him, and looked to him for payment. When Kenyon was brought before that court Hill attended as a witness, and i, was ad- mitted that the actual terms of the dissolution were that Kenyon would pa' all thelVigan accountra and Hill the St. Helens portion. Plaintiff afterwards saw Hill in the street, and Hill then said he would pay him.—Mr. Byrom said that unless this could be proved Mr. Swift ought not to say it.— Mr. Swift went on to say that Hill admitted himself morally liable.—His Honour said he was disposed to leave the matter to the moral feelings of Mr. Hill. There was no doubt it was a partnership debt. He would feave it in Mr. Hill's bands if lie admitted he was morally lieble.—Mr. Byrom: But we do not.-11i5 Honour: I will leave it with them to arrange it themselves. .

div.head: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD,
div.p: PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD,

The usual monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday evening, at the board-room, Derby- street, Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., presiding. There were also present Messrs. C. Spencely (vice-chairman), :f. Johnson Brown, J. Sanders, and T. P. Hewitt; with Mr. IL Cross (clerk), and Mr. W. Lloyd (attendance officer.) ATTENDANCE OFFICER'S REPORT. The attendance officer (Mr. Win. Lloyd) repotted that he bad visited the several schools in his district, also the Huyton and Roby schools. He had ssrved notices on the parents of 41 children and also visited the parents of 112 children who had been absent from or irregularly attending school. The two summonses which stood for hearing on the IStla inst., as per last report, were disposed of on that 'date, and the four summonses which be was ordered to take out on the 26th ult, were disposed of on the 81h inst., the usual fine of ss. including costs being inflicted in each case. At a committee meeting he eras instructed to report respect- ing four boys who could not ue,got to school. Two of the boys have since been committed by the magistrates to a re- I, formatory school for five years each. With respect to the other two—William Donohue and John King—he reported that the former had made 34 attendances out of 13S times the school had been open. He firmly believed that that boy could not be got to school except he was taken either by I his mother or brother. The boy King is not on the register at the school. be not having attended for a long time. The mother says she can do no good with hirri.—lt was resolved ' that summonses for attendance orders be taken out against the parents of Donohue and King, that being the first step I, towards getting them into an industrial school. THE ATTENDANCE AT THE SCHOOLS. Miss Duke, mistress of the girls' school, reported that the average attendance of scholars in her department for the previous week was 66 as compared with 66 in the corre- sponding week of last year.—The CHAIRMAN: Have you got any children back who were not attending through the fs,ver ?—Miss DUES: : Yes. Two came back this morning. —Miss Macgregor reported that the average attendance in the infant school for the previous week was 55 as corn-

RAINFITLL REFOIN CLUB.

---- - On Monday last Mr. C. Rawlins, of Rainhill, delivered a lecture entitled "Free Trade and Fair Trade, a non-pelitical discussion," in the Rainhill National Schools, under the auspices of the Rainhill Reform Club. The chair Was occu- pied by Mr. G. W. Rawlins (the chairman of the club and SOU of the lecturer), and there was a good attendance. The CHAIHMLI7, in the course of a brief address, con- gratulated the Liberals of Rainhill upon the holding of that meeting. That lecture was the first of a series of lectures and papers, the object of which was the dissemination of sound political views and the spread of Liberalism. He then introduced The LECTURER, who, before delivering his address, re- ferred to the formation of ii. Reform Club and of a Conserva- tive Club in Rainhill, and considered they would a source of very geeat social pleasare and political advantage. The object of the Reform Club was to unite those who were in favour of political progress, so that whenever the time for political action came they might know where to find one another and be able to present an unbroken front to their political enemies. (Applause.) He then proceeded to deliver his lecture, observing that although the subject of his lecture was one of the principal questions which at the present moment was dividing Liberals and ConservatiVes, it ought not in any way to be considered a political question, but merely a subject for fasts and figures, profit and loss, and household expenditure. Free Trade meant the right of every man to buy well, and ,to expend his wages and income in the free and open market without let or hindrance. He then dwelt at length on the history of the Free Trade move- ment, and referred to the hopes expressed at the time by its ' advocates the other nations would follow the example of Great Britain, but which hopes had not been realised. He strongly deprecated England following the example of other I countries and returning to partial protection. The argu- ments of the fair traders was that it trade was to be free it should be so on both sides ; and that if free imports existed I \on one side, and imports fettered by duty on the other, any trade between the parties wonld be unfair. The fair traders' definition was truer tha i they were willing to admit. By the return to partial protection, which the fair traders advocated, i they did not seem to understand their definition, for as a Imatter of fact Fair Trade was an impossibility where a ; custom-house existed. Mr. Rawlins next referred to a ?,veial .! of the recent speeches of the principal advocates of Fair I Trade, and showed, in an able manner, the absurdity of I many of their arguments in support of their V1C904. With Iregard to their advice that England should follow the 1 example of other countries, he said he trusted the policy of England would always be her own policy—an independent policy, and not dictated from without, a policy of doing right because it was right, and as a country having the sacred mission of teaching other nations how to live.—The usual votes of thanks closed the proceedings.

Then speaking of the legislative control over the traffic. II a summons is taken out against a publican for permitting drunkenness, and he is convicted, his license is endorsed.; if twice in the year he is liable to lose his license. I asked an experienced magistrate how often that power had been exercised, and he said be never saw it exercised once." I reepectfully recommend Justice Kay's remarke to the consideration of Mr. Robert Davies, who at the recent Tory meeting had the audacity to say that "dear Gilbert had never brought a bad. thing to Warrington." I What never? Has not his whole life been devoted to ex- tending the drink traffic in this and other towns? and all thoughtful men are agreed that it (the traffic) lo a fruitful ' source of vice and Crime as well as being the cause of much ' bodily sickness and premature deaths, and the only legisla- tive feat I remember the Hector of Home Secretaries to have performed was to assist the great brewer to sell his I drink by prolonging the hours for drinking. Vo doubt the Chairman could say under these circumstances "I am I present with you, in unity with you, and united with you, dic., and he concludes, with God's help we are determined to I accomplish these objects. Could Charles Bradlamgh be more irreligious ?—Yours, dec., J. H. G. PUDDLERS' STRIKE IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—I should esteem it a great favour if you would insert this letter in next issue. I saw a statement in your paper last Saturday week, written by a person who signed himself "Paddle," in which the writer seems to rejoice at the opportunity which the unfortunate dispute at Bewsey affords him of venting his opleen and scurrilous charges against Mr. Morris. Some of them I shall endeavour to refute. In the first place he attempts to allow that Mr. Morris is not juetified in taking 21. per ton off paddlers when he gives them all mine to fettle with. I say be is, and it is the custom in this country where all mine is given to a puddler to fettle his furnace with to take 6d. per ton off him because he gets an equivalent to 6d. in the superior material sent to him, which, if properly used, will produce more iron which ,aill compensate him for the 6d. taken of. "Paddle" seems to ignore the fact that other wire manufacturers are only paying 7s. 31. per ton for common fencing wire. How then is the Pearson and Knowles Co. to compete with those masters if they are to pay more per ton than they ? "Paddle" seems to forget that by Mr. Morris's judicious management in 1879 and 1980 he kept 1 the Hallam and Bewsey Forges working six days a week I when other works were closed in the district through de- pression of trade. All those benefits" Paddle" forgets. He talks about custom. It is quite evident from what he knows about it, it is very little. As a puddler of 23 years' ex- perience, I always found where all mine fettling was given to paddlers to use he had 6d. per ton less than he who bad all bull-dog. That is the recognised rule anywhere in this country. I cannot see that " Paddle" has proved that Mr. Morris has broken through that custom. With regard to the next question which "Paddle" asks, is it the custom for paddlers who work wire iron to be paid extra? the question is easily answered. They are paying 78 Pd. per ton in this town (Warrington) for puddling common fencing iron. Other iron masters are having the work done for 75. 3d. per ton, or 6d. per ton less than the masters in Warrington pay. "Paddle" cannot blame Mr. Morris for adopting a custom Which was broken by others. Ile never yet asked the puddlers at Bewsey to work wire iron for 7s. 3d. per ton. If "Paddle" would use his influence with the puddlers to sub- mit their case to arbitration I would give him credit for being sincere. Ho next states that the puddlers at Messrs. Monks' works get more money at 7s. Pd. per ton than the puddleraat Bewsey who received Bs. per ton, for the same quantity of work brought out. That statement is like the others ; he has drawn upon his imagination, for it so happens I have a puddler's pay note by me from Monks, and I cannot see wherethey get more money than Bewsey paddlers. I think, sir, such statements as" Paddle " makes are calculated to mislead the public and to injure the men who are out. I think, sir, I have trespassed too much upon your space. Hoping you will find this a place in your Saturday issue.— I remain, yours truly, JOHN GRIFFITHS, 6, Catherine-street, Warrington. JOHN ALLEN, THOMAS HAYNES, THOMAS TROMAN, Foremen, Bewsey Iron Works.

Will qe please explain the privileges at I%he works, and not ebehinikntpowsbrr °dig give half the truth? And how can tell, never having seen the fettling, whether it increases the labour or not? I have worked, it ; Mr. Capper has net ; and I would rather work with the old fettling. When he talks about the merits of the case let hint he sure, as he either knows nothing about it, or his statement is deMerately false, when he states they work wive iron and hoop iron at Dallarn for 78. 91. per ton, as they never did work either class of iron at Dallarn, neither is there any 7s.'d. per ton paid at Dallarn; the enly prices paid at Dalian: being. 7s. 3d. and Ss. 3d. Mr. Jones states our wages have always been regulated by their Beard. Surely Mr. Jones cannot be serious, because all the changes I have named in my last were made when no change was made in any other district, and our employers wou,d not thm recognise the right el the Board or anyone else to interfere between theta and us. Both Messrs. Capper and Jones condemn us now; but how about the cendert of the firm in refusisg us a , day off so that we might decide what we would do? " No," said they, "if you de not come to work, come for your money." Is this the display of friendly feeling referred to by Mr. Capper batwer..n Bewsey managers and !nen, and the Kind, of conciliation he advocates? I do not hesitate to say that had we been 1-.. lowed Monday, instead of being treated as we were, the dispute could have been settled without difficulty. But this conduct, along with the interference of outsiders, has made matters worse, and we shall never agree to arbitration before a Board whose officers can write as they do about tint of which they know so little ; but -we will trust to our own abilities to obtain what we want, and if Lancashire is to be governed by a Board it shall be a local one establitcaed by ourselves, the members of which we can place confidence in, and give support te. Hoping you will excuse this long letter, and with thanks for your fair- ness towards Iss,l remain, yours, &c, PADDLE. , WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY LIEBATINGr , SOCIETY AND THE TORY SECESSION. , Sir,—With your permission, I desire to make a remark or two upon the proceedings of the Warrington Parliamentary Debating Society, a full report of which will no doubt appear in your Saturday's edition, and although the impar- tial and just ruling of the Speaker was many times referred to, I shall be cbliged if you will allow me to disabuse—by means of a letter—the minds of the public, who cannot help being led away with the idea that the Speaker is wholly responsible for the action of the Tories. The only inference which can be drawn from the letter which will appear is an impeachment of the Speaker's ruling, and, sir, the iasult offered to Dr. Iluson-More cannot be too strongly refuted. I, as one who objected as strongly as the members of the Opposition to the course of argument taken by severalmem- bets and particularly the right hon. member for Northampton in the debate OD the oaths' question, mean to say that the quotations used and the non-interference of the Speaker was strictly parliamentary, and was to my mind but another evidence of the wonderful knowledge possessed by the Speaker, in the difficult duty of leading and. conduct- ing debates. The scene which occurred during the first night's debate on this question suggested to my nfind the well-known lines of Robert Burns— "Oh wad some wan the giftie gie us." Putting aside the mud throwing and odium and the attempt to hook on to the whole Liberal party the religious or anti- religions opinions of a few men, intended by the publication of the letter to the Speaker, I deem an apology or public explanation necessary from the Leader of the Opposition for the slight cast upon the Speaker's conduct, not to be merely published in the neutral organ but in the local papers generally. Thanking you in prospective for the insertion of this letter, I enclose my card and beg to remain THE HON. MEMBER FOR WILLENHALL. Warrington, November 24ti___

oaths in this country. There was always a class of people, with a certain amount of superstitious feeling, and it was necessary that some superstitions be kept over them. And that was afforded in the form of oath which they took to their God. (Hear, hear.) He read some of Mr. Bradlaugh's extreme views on Christianity, and said it would do no good to allow such a man help to make the laws of this great nation.—The Home Secretary said it would have been an everlasting scandal to Northampton not to have returned Mr. Bradlaugh, considering the question they had before them. The question now was not whether Atheists should be admitted into Parliament or not, but had we any right to debar any man, whatever his principles might be, of his rights as a citizen of this country. (Hear, hear.) They had no such right. If that right existed why was it not used against the Roman Catholics and the Jews? Be- cause every honest man felt he was doing a grave injustice in keeping a man who paid taxes, and was loyal to the Crown, from participating in the benefits of office. Mr. Bradlaugh had been allowed to affirm in courts of law, and if his word could be taken there it would possess the same weight if he took an affirmation of allegiance to the Crown and Constitution. The gentlemen on the Conservative side of the House professed to be trinitarians. The Jews denied the divinity of the Saviour, and was it a greater sin for a man to deny two parts than it was for a man to deny the existeace of one? They had already admitted men to sit who said the Saviour was not divine, and therefore com- mitted one of the greatest offences against the doctrines of the Church of England, bat when they were asked to admit a man who denied the first part of the trinity their indigna- tion rose like froth to the top of a beer barrel. (Applause.) How any Roman Catholic or Jew, who was at all acquainted with the history of his people, could vote against carrying out the principle of civil and religious freedom a little fur- ther was past his comprehension. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)—The members for Woodstock, Stoke-on-Trent, North-East Lancashire, Mr. Stirrup, Radnor Boroughs, and Mr. Smith continued the debate, which was concluded by the Secretary for India. A vote was then taken, and the Speaker declared the "ayes" to have the majority.—On the motion of the Prime Minister, the House resolved itself into committee, and the standing orders were suspended to allow the presence of strangers. The Speaker was unanimously Voted to the chair. He said he had received the following

argued that as the two weights which had, professedly, been adjusted by the Superintendent, were the next day found to be incorrect, it was just possible that the weights for which he was now summoned had never been properly set right when they had been in the hands of Mr. Barker. Superin- tendent Barker said he bad had to do with weights during 25 years, and he had on more than ens occasion found them incorrect within 24 hours of the time at which they had been adjusted. This was owing to the shameful usage to i which they were frequently put n grocers and other shops, where the assistants were in the habit of using them as ham- mers when they bad not one handy. Defendant was fined 205., and 12s. costs. YOUTHFUL DEPEAVITT.—EIIen Andrews, aged 13, was charged with stealing 4s. 6d., the money of George Griffin, butcher, High-street, Wavertree, on the 22n4 inst.—From the statement of the prosecutor's wife, it appeared that she went into the back yard, leaving the prisoner, who was acting as servant, in the house. Andrews fastened the door leading into the dwelling so that her mistress could not get in, and. abstracted the money from the till. The robbery was discovered, and on the prisoner being charged, she ad- mitted her s from the tillt.—fMrs.G b e._ riffieftohrsstaprsouteidsehr w e had s sentm missed to gaol 14 days, and at the end of that term, ordered to be committed to a reformatory.

lays. ALLEGED BREAKING INTO A Dventaiten-uousu. —Sarah Den Ward was charged with breaking into the house of lef rs. Elizabeth Jones, No. 9, Chatham-street, and stealing leurpence, a pair of gins, a jet chain, and a shawl.— The prosecutrix said that on the previous Wednesday morn- ' ng she went away from home, and quitted the house about eght o'clock, leaving her three children, of whom the eldest vas eleven years of age, within. She saw that the back door and windows were securely fastened, and closed the front door behind her as she went out. She returned about a quarter to three, and tried the front door, but could not open it, and then went round to the back, when she found that both the door and window had been opened. There was a latch to the window, which had been undone. She entered the house and examined it, and missed the clogs produced, which were kept on a shelf in the kitchen; the shawl, the jet chain, and 41. in cover, which had been kept in a tin box in the cupboard. The house was upset throug,hout. She detected footmarks on the dresser, which stood directly beneath the back kitchen window.—A woman named Caunce, also residing in Chatham-street, deposed to seeing the prosecutrix leave the house and securely close to door behind her.—Jane Jones, 10 years of age, child of the prose- nutria, stated that she was left in the house by her mother, with her little sister and brother, early on Wednesday. To- wards nine o'clock she went to school, with her sister and brother. She went out by the front doer, which she fas- tened securely behind her. She came hack about four o'clock, and then foend that her mother had already returned.— Michael Boyle, a rag dealer, living at 9, Chatham-street, said that on Wednesday, about two o'clock, he was at the back of the street, near the house occupied by Mrs. Jones, when the prisoner saw him, and asked him to buy a pair of clogs, now produced. He offered her 4d. for them, and sub- sequently gave her 411—The Inspector of Police: Did not it strike you that they were a pair of good clogs not worn at all 7—The Clerk: What could you make of them if you sold them P—l could not make more than 6d. of them.—The In- spector: Why, the irons are worth that much.—The Clerk : Did she say where she got them from 7—Witness said that he did not ask any questions. The prisoner told him that she wanted to dispose of the clogs, because they were a rnis- At. He had since given them up to P.C. Pitt —P.C. Pitt said that on Thursday last he apprehended the prisoner at a house in Chapel-entry, off Lugedale-road, Widnes.—The prisoner, who had nothing to say in defence, was committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions. WEDNESDAY—Before Mr. E. K. Muspratt (chairman), and Mr. A. Fletcher. Onee DOO LESS !—Moses Bate was summoned for keeping a dog without a licence.— P.C. Pitt said that on the 15th inst., he called at the defendant's, and there saw a dog for which he had no licence. Defendant alleged that the dog was too young to need one, but he had since killed it.—De- fendant was fined 53. and costs. WIDNES Auezons.—Mary Hannon and Mary Clarke were proved to have fought in Waterloo-road, on the 13th nit., whilst under the influence of drink.—Superintendent Barker said that was the eighth appearance of Clarke before the Court during the year.—Each defendant was ordered to enter into sureties to keep the peace three months, herself in £lO and one in £5, or in default be sent to gaol for 14 days. A CORNER MAN FlNED.—William Kilroy was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, on the evidence of P.C. Pitt, for having, on the 15th inst., obstructed Ann-street West, and refused to leave when requested. THE ScHoor, BOARD AT Woux —The following parents were summoned by the Wid es School Board for not sending their children to school :—Thomas Dillon, Thomas Kerley, Thomas Wele'i, Peter Riley, John Riley, Evan Roberts, Daniel Brannon, and Thomas Bowyer.—Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the Board, appeared to prosecute, and the cases were proved ley the attendance officers, Messrs. Davies, Wood, and Joynson. Each defendant was ordered to pay 55., in- cluding costs.—Mr. Denby asked the Bench to make an order for the committal of a lad named Simon, the son of John Kilroy, to an industrial school. The youth was an in- corrigible one. His father was unable to manage him; he had been brought before the magistrates several times; and the members of the School Board were fully convinced that the parent had done all in his power to get his lad to attend school. The youngster had formed the companionship of a number of bad lads. Mr. Danbs- made a similar application in the case of a youth named 'Cinemas Coleman. Mr. Davies, attendance officer, said he had done his best to get the boy to school, hut without avail. The boy was in the habit of staying away from home a fortnight at a time, and sleeping in outhouses. In fact, he was quite beyond the control of his perents, and the father had expressed his willingness that he should be sent to an industrial school.—An order was made that each of the boys should be sent to St. George's I Industrial School, Liverpool, until he is 16 years of age. THE THEFT FROM A. LOOOING-110II3E. Patrick McDermott was charged with stealing a satchel, containing a watch, value £5, and 18s., belonging to Joseph Mills, lodging-house keeper, Oxford-street. The evidence of the prosecutrix showed that about a fortnight ago, the prisoner lodged at her house, and on the Friday told her he bad obtained work at the Widnes Foundry and should commence there on the Monday morning. She according agreed to supply him with further food. On Saturday she saw him go into the parlour, and on coming out noticed that he had something under his arm. She then examined the room, ' and found that the articles mentioned bad been stolen. She raised an alarm, on which the prisoner ran out at the back door.—P.C. Pitt proved apprehending the prisoner at Run- corn.—McDermott was sentented to CIA InOnth's imprison- ment, with hard labour. A WIDNES BUTCHER FINED £s.—John Wilkinson, trading under the high qouuding name of the British Work- man .41 4mcllcan Fresh Meat Co., in Hutchinson-street, 4was ellarged with having, on the 28th Octoker, had in his possession eight sheep plucks which were unfit for feed, —Mr. W. T. Husband said he appeared for the Widnes Local Board, by whom the prosecution had been instituted. The plucks were selected out of a number of others by Mr. hee; John Dickson, meat inspector, and then examined by Mr. Robinson, veterinary surgeon, who pronounced them unfit for ' food. The meat was taken before a justice of the peace, who ordered it to be destroyed. The proceedings were taken( under the 116 and 117 section of the Public Health Act,' which allowed a penalty of £2O for every animal carcase, so that the accumulative penalty in this particular case would amount to £l6O. Ile hoped that the Bench would take notice that defendant's shop was situated in a poor locality, where meat of a cheap character was specially provided to meet the requirements of the wotking classes ; and in this case it was offered for sale under a high sounding name.— Mr. Dickson and Mr. Alfred Robinson were called in support of the case. The latter stated that defendant told him the plucks had been passed by one of the meat inspectors at Liverpool, on which he replied that if this were so, the man required to be taught his business.—The Chairman : This is a very serious offence, and defendant will be fined £5 and the costs. Mr. Husband's fee and the costs of Mr. Robinson were also allowed. A DRUNKEN LDRRYIKAN.—Henry Grace was, on the evidence of P.C. Strickland, fined 10s. and is. 6d. costs for having been found drunk in Warrington-road, on the after- noon of the sth inst., whilst in charge of two horses and a

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY :—Before Mr. Wm. Bankes (Chairman), and Mr. Thomas. Mn. MARSHALL'S EXPERIENCE AS AN EVANGELIST . John Nockton, a tall, powerful man, was summoned for using violent and abusive language, calculated to produce a breach of the peace, towards Mr. George Marshall, druggist, High-street, on the 13th inst. Complainant said that" they" bad an evangelical mission at Rock Savage every Sabbath; and on the 13th inst., about half-past five in the afternoon they went out, as had been their custom during the last 16 months, to have an open-air service. They sang three or four evangelical hymns, and then a ring was formed, and he knelt down to pray in the centre. Whilst he was doing so he heard a noise as of several men coming on to the scene, who were drunken and tried to overpower his.voice. Nock- ton was one of them, but as witness was praying at the time, be scarcely knew wl- at were the words he used. He only heard one sentence clearly, and it was "I will have you out of that." Ile then raised his hand and said, "Now, young man, be quiet: I am not speaking to you; I am talking to Jesus." Defendant replied, "But I am talking to you." Several young men about saw that defendant meant mis- chief, and they sprang forward and thus prevented his giv- ing a blow. Nockton struck one of the young men in the chest. A struggle afterwards followed amongst the young men. He had summoned defendant as he caused the affray to commence. Defendant and his four companiona were drunk. However, as defendant's father-in-law and his own wife were dangerously ill, complainant added that he thought the proceedings taken thus far would answer the I purpose, and prevent a repetition of such conduct, if the Bench would kindly permit him to withdraw the charge on condition that Nockton paid the court expenses. Defendant had expressed his regret, and done all in his power since the affair happened to make reparation.—The Chairman: Under all the circumstan;es we allow the case to be withdrawn. SCHOOL BOARD PROSECUTION.—JOhn TOTTIkinSOn, Gran- ville-street, was summoned by the Runcorn School Board, for not sending his child Hannah to school.—Mr. Bowyer, school attendance officer, proved the case, and defendant was ordered to pay 55., including costs. A FOCI}MOIITHED WOMAN—Mary Riley was fined lOs , and 9s. 6d. costs, on the evidence of Sergeant Walley, for using abusive and profane language in High-street, on the I 11th inst. A SON NEGLECTING HIS OLD FATHER.—A young man, named Samuel Littler, of Moore, was summoned by the Runcorn Board of Guardians for neglecting to contribute to the support of his father, who is an elderly and infirm man, chargeable to the common fund of the Runcorn Union.—Mr. Thomas Houghton, collector to the Guardians, said defend- ant was a bricklayer, and his father had now been charge- able to the Union for two years. During eighteen months Littler had not paid a single farthing towards the support of his father.—Defendant admitted that, when in work, he earned 30s. per week.—The Chairman said an order would be made upon defenflant to pay 3s. a week, and 14s. 61 costs. If defendant let the guardians know when he was out of work he would not be rrquired to pay in those par- ticular weeks. THCRSDAY.—Before Messrs. A. Thomas and C. %V. Hazlehurst. STEALING A COAT.—John White, a sailor, was charged with stealing a coat, value 125., the property of Mr. Patrick Collins, clothier,Church-street.—Prisoner, visited the prise- cutor's shop on Wednesday, with two other sailers, and bought a shirt and a sailor's bag. After he had gone, a coat which had been hanging at the door was missed, and was afterwards found in the prisoner's bag, at Pegg's boarding house.—White was therefore taken into custody, and was now fined 205., and 20s. costs.

lurry. DEBTS% ON lACENsED Pu,Rstisf.s.—John Monaghan and Terence Matthews (tha former of whom did not appear) were charged with having been drunk on the licensed pre- 1 rnises known as the Norton Arms.—P.C. Graham said that ' on the night of the sth inst., about a quarter to nine eeclock, be was standing übon' 12 yards from the Norton Arms public house, when he heard a great noise in the bar. He , ntered, and saw the two defendants fighting upon the floor.—The Superintendent said this was the seventh appear- ance of Matthews, who was fined 103. and costa.--James Tilley, the keeper of the Norton Arms, was next charged with keeping a disorderly house on the night mentioned in the last offence.—P.C. Graham gave similar evidence, and was supported by P.C. Rogers.—Mr. Bartlett defended, and maintained that the wife of his client had done nothing more than her duty. On the night of the -sth, Monaghan, one of the defendants in the last case, was in the house having a glass of beer, when Matthews, who is a quarrel- some, litigious fellow, came in and asked the landlady for something to drink. She refused to supply him, and advised him to go borne. Matthews then became enraged, and picked a quarrel with Monaghan, who he gave a severe blow which knocked him down. The dispute was only an affair of a moment, and it would have been no use for Mrs. Tilley to rush out and call "police." as it was generally found that on such occasions they did not happen to be upon the spot. (Laughter.) Unfortunately, at the particular mom( . P.C. Graham was near at hand, and what he saw led hi to suppose that disorderly conduct was being per- mitted the landlady.—Mrs. Tilley, Ellen Pierce, James Monagl and James Potter, of Ann-street, were called for the defe. —The Chairman said the case was a somewhat difficult' to decide, as very much depended upon how long the t, rrel between the two men had gone on before the police , dered the house. The Superintendent had good grounds for bringing tbe matter before them, but, under the peculiar circumstances, the Bench had decided to give de- fendantthe bentfi:' of the doubt and dismiss the case, but he must pay the costs. div.head: WIDNES SCITOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCITOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon, at the offices in Victoria-road. Mr. T. Sutton-Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. Holloway, James Clarke, Messrs. Hartland, Shaw, Davis, Deacon, Brock, Bradshaw, and Danby (clerk.)

DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. The report of this committee was read by Mr. DEACON, and stated that during October, the number of cases summoned before the the committee was 430, of which 98 were appli- cations for payment of fees, and 332 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 87 cases, and 11 applications were refused. There had been 16 prosecutions before the magistrates, in all of which convic- tions had been obtained, and two children bad been sent to industrial schools. The committee recommended that they should be empowered to hire the Lacey-street school-room, in which to hold their meetings, at a cost not exceeding five shillings per time. Mr. Deacon remarked, at the conclusion of reading the report, that the committee had thought it very undesirable, especially du,ting the winter time when parents frequently came to the Board offices in wet clothes, that they should have no place but the staircase in which to stand until their cases were decided. Under the proposed arrange- ment, the people would be able to sit down in the hall con- nected with Lacey-street schools. The CHAIRMAN, in secondly the adoption of the report, which was adopted, said he dil so with very much pleasure.

SCIIOOL MAXAOXMENT COMMITTEE. The Rev. GEO. Hou.owlk read the report of the com- mittee, which was passed. The Simm's Cross managera recommended that Edward Glover and Wm. Winn be en- gaged as monilors ; the West Bank Manggers, that Clara MaTher and George F. Parr be en- gaged as monitors; and that the indentures of Arthur G. Davies be cancelled. DISTRICT OF WIDNES. THE PUBLIC LIBRARIES' ACTS, 1855-1866-1871-1877. Widnes, Nov. 17th, 1881. [Recived November 22, 1880.] To JAMES CROSS, ESQ., M.1.0.E., Chairman of the Widnes Local Board. Dear Bir,—We, the undersigned Ratepayers of Widnes, humbly ask you to take the necessary stens, as required and statea by you at the General Board Meesing, and as required by Act of Parliament. And we humbly ask you to call a Public Meeting as to the desirability of forming and having a " Free Public Library "in Widnes, and paid for out of a small rate. It is useless in saying anything upon the subject of a free library being wanted in Widnes to you, for there is no one knows better than yourself the requirement and want of chances in books and reading rooms for working men in their leisure hours to educate themselves, and to fill their minds with useful knowledge. Also, that business men may lay hold of books which are very often very scarce and very dear, for a small pay- ment. We feel sure If we gain your sympathy in this movement (which we believe we have) we shall also have ycur valuable help in carry lug out the object to its fulfillment. We are, dear Sir. Yours respectfully, James Ruddiman, 16, Widnes-road, chem'cal labourer: John Mass, 55, Midwood-street, chemical labourer ; Thomas Prescot, 38, Widnes-road, labourer; Wm. J. Mahon, 9, Saxon- terrace, clerk ; E. Simmonds, collector: H. Beacham, railway Inspector; Henry Cla.ke, Peel-house-lane, Farnworth ; Thomas Hewitt, 31, Lacey-street; Frank Barton, 5, Midwood-street ; Wm. Pinnington, 10, Widnes-road ; Edward Taylor. 41, West- street; John Betney, 121, Mersey-road; John Walsh, 1, Carey- street ; Thomas Lancaster, Foster-street; 11. Lancaster, 116, Kent-street; Thomas Hunt, 70, Appleton-in-Widnes ; John W. Holden, 37, Wellington-street; Samuel Cartwright, Ditton ; Thomas Hall 24, Mersey-road ;J. 0. Rhodes, 26, Mersey-road; Charles Benbow, 78, Mersey-road • William Melvin, 42, Mersey-road; William Farmer, 90, Hurst-street: Hugh Brown, licensed victualler; James Birchall. draper; Horatio Syred, pawnbroker: Joseph Stones, App:eton; Joseph itetney. 55, Waterloo-road; Thomas Caldwell, 16, Deacon read; James Norris, 5, Elliott-street; William Henry Parsons, 33, Choi- mondeley-street ; Alexander Bell, joiner, 12, Midwood-street ; Evan Hughes, joiner, Luntsheath ; James Rimmer, Frederick- street. In accordance with the above requisition, I hereby call a PUBLIC MEETING of the Ratepayers for the district of Widnes, to be held in the VOLUNTEER HALL, WIDNES, on TUESDAY, the 6th day of DECEMBER, 1881, at half-past Seven o'clock in the evening. JAMES CROSS, Chairman, Widnes Local Board. Note.—Only persons assessed to, and paying the General District Rate for the township of Widnes, have a right to be present and vote at the above meeting.

IN PARLIAMENT.—SERSION 1882. SAINT HELENS (CORPORATION) WATER. (Construction of Waterworks—Compulsory Purchase of Land—Extension of Water Limits—Levy and Alteration of Rates and Charges—Borrowing of Money—Amend- ment. Repeal, and Incorporation of Acts). NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN. that Application is intended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing Session by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the town of Saint Helens, in the County of Lancaster (hereinafter called the Corporation), for leave to bring in a Bill for all or some of the following purposes (that is to say) : To empower the Corporation to make and maintain the works hereinafter described, or some of them, that is to say- 1. The Kirkby Pumping Station.—A shaft or well (to be sunk to an uncertain depth) with pumps, engines, and appliances connected therewith, wholly situate in the township of Kirkby, in the parish of Walton-on-the- Hill, in and near the south-east corner of a field, which adjoins, on the south side thereof, Old Rough Cottage, stack yard, and croft, which lie and abut on the northerly side of Old Rough-lane, and which field belongs, or is reputed to belong, to the Earl of Bettors, and is in the occupation of Thomas Owen. 2. An Aqueduct or Line of Pipes. eommencing in the said township and parish, at the said intended shaft or well, and terminating in the township of Knowsley, In the parish of Huyton, by a junction with the aque- duct hereinafter described in Moss-lane, at a point fourteen chains or thereabouts south of the junction of Scarisbrick-brow with Old Molly's-lane. which aque- duct will be wholly situate in the townships of Kirkby and Knowsley, and parishes of Walton-on-the-Hill and Huyton. 3. The Knowsley Pumping Station.—A shaft or well (to be sunk to an uncertain depth) with pumps, engines, and appliances connected therewith, wholly eituate in the township of Knowsley, in the parish of Huyton, in the north-easterly portion of a field abutting on the north- west on the brook which forms the b.iundary of the townships of Kirkby and Knowsley, and abutting as to part of such field, and on the easterly side thereof on Moss-lane, and on the north-easterly side thereof on the garden belonging, or attached to a house o: cottage in Moss-lane, in the occupation of one Thomas Ratcliffe, and which field belongs, or is reputed to belong, to the Earl of Derby, and is in the occupation of Joseph Hewitt. 4. An Aqueduct or Line of Pipes, commencing in the said township of Knowsley and parish of Huyton, at the last-mentioned intended theft or well, and terminating in the township of Becleston, in the parish of Prescot, in Holt-lane, at its junction with Scholes-lane, end by a junction with the existing aqueduct of the Corpora- tion, which intended aqueduct will be wholly situate in the townships of Knowsley and Eceleston, and parishes of Huyton and Present. All which intended works will be wholly situate In the Jounty of Lancaster. Together with all proper and necessary wells, shafts, tun- nel., drifts, edits, pipes, salves, syphons, hydrants, junctions, tanks, basins, engines, pumps, buildings, embankments. roads, and other works connected with the shafts or wells, aqueducts and works aforesaid, and which may be necessary or proper for taking, pumping. impounding, using, and distributing the waters intended to be taken. To empower the Corporation for the purposes of the intended works and Act, to purchase or acquire by compulsion or agree- ment, or to take on lease, any lands, houses, or buildings, or to appropriate any lands, houses, or buildings belonging to them In the townships, parishes, and county aforesaid, and any rights, or easements in, over, or connected with any lands, houses, or buildings in the townships, parishes, and county aforesaid, and on the sale of lands to reserve water and other rights. To empower the Corporation to take, pump, divert, impound, appropriate, and use for the purposes of their water under- taking, or other the purposes of the intended Act, all springs, streams, and waters which may be found In, upon, or under any lands acquired or held by the Corporation under the powers of the intended Act, or which can. or may be taken, or intercepted by the intended works or some of them. ,To empower the Corpomtioo to deviate in the construction of the intended works laterally and vertically to the extent to be shown on the plans and sections to be deposited as herein- after mentioned or to be defined in the intended Act. To authorise the Oxporatlon to lay down, maintain, alter, and renew mains, pipes, culverts, sewers, and drains in, through, along. under, across, and over anjs public highways, streets, roads, streams, paths, tramways and railways, and for the purposes of the intended Act to break up, cross, alter, divert, stop up (either temporarily or permanently), and inter- fere with tends, streets, highways, courts, alleys, footpaths, bridges, tramways, railways, sewers, drains, streams, brooks, water-courses, mains, pipes, and telegraphs within the parishes, townships, and places at oresaid. To extend the limits of the Corporation for supplying water to all places within the said townships of Kirkby and Knowsley. To empower the Corporation for all or any of the purposes of the intended Act to demand, recover, and levy rates, rents, and charges for and in respect of the supply of water, to in- crease or vary existing rates, rents, and charges, and confer ex- emptions therefrom, and to apply any money belonging to, or under the control of the Corporation to all or any of the objects and purposes of the intended Act, and to borrow money for the purposes of the intended Act, and to mortgage or charge the rates, rents, tolls, or charges levied or leviable by them, and their Gas and Water undertakings, lands and Property, or some of them, as security therefor, with power to issue debentures, debenture stock, and annuity certificates, -charge- able upon the securities in af resaid. or any of them, and to make provision for the repayment of money to be so borrowed. To vary or extinguish all existing rights and privileges, which would or might in any way prevent or interfere with or delay the accomplishment of any of the objects of the intended Act, and to confer other rights and privileges. To repeal or amend all or some of the provisions of the follow- ing Local Act, and pub to Acts of a local character. namely The St. Bele is Improvement Act, 1869. The Local Govern- ment Board's Provisional Orders Confirmation (Belper Union, etc.) Act. 1877. The Local Government Board's Provisional Orders Confirmation (Abingdon, etc.) Act, 1878. The Local Government Board's Provisional Orders C,onfirniation (Aber- gavenny Union, etc ) Aet 1879, and all other Acts relating to the Corporation. The Liverpool Corporation Waterworks Act, 1847. The Liverpool Corporation Waterworks Act, 1880, and all Acts relating to the Waterworks undertaking of the Mayor. Aldermen, and Citizens of the City of Liverpool. To incorporate with or without alterations and amendments all or some of ti-se provisions of the following Public Acts, namely: The Commissioners' Clauses Act, 1847, the lands Clauses Consolidation Acts, 1845, 1860, and 1869. The Water- works' Clauses Acts, 1647 and 1863. The Local Loans Act, 1875, and the Provisions of the Railways' 018.1/86.9 Consolidation Act, 1945, with respect to the temporary oc.ppation of lauds and all Acts amending the same respectively or any of them, and all or some of the Provisions or the St. Helens Improvement Act, 1869. On or before the 30th day of November instant. duplicate plans, and sections, and books of reference to such plans, to- gether with a espy of this notice as published in the London Gazette, will be deposited for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace for the County of Lancaster, at his office at Preston, and on or before the same day a copy of so much of the said plans, sections, and books of reference as relates to the several parishes in or through which the said intended works are pro- posed to be made, together with a copy of this notice, will on or before the said 30th day of November be deposited with the Clerk of each such parish at his residence. Printed copies of the intended Act or Bill, will, on or before the 21st day of December next, be deposited in the Private Bill Office a the House of Commons. Dated this Fourth day of November. 1881.. THOMAS BREW'S, Town Clerk, Bt. Helens, SHARPE, PARKES% PRITCFIARD, &SHARP% 9, Bridge-street, Westminister, Parliamentaty Agents.
